topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: 'New Duck Disease' (Infectious Serositis), an acute to chronic septicemic disease of 1-to-8-week-old ducklings characterized by fibrinous pericarditis, perihepatitis, airsacculitis, and torticollis, is caused by:
options: Riemerella anatipestifer
Avibacterium paragallinarum
Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae
Pasteurella multocida subsp. septica
explanation: Riemerella anatipestifer (formerly Pasteurella anatipestifer / Moraxella anatipestifer) is a non-motile, non-spore-forming Gram-negative rod belonging to the family Weeksellaceae (order Flavobacteriales) that causes Infectious Serositis ('New Duck Disease') in ducks, geese, and turkeys.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Infectious Bovine Keratoconjunctivitis (IBK / 'Pinkeye'), the most common contagious ocular disease of cattle worldwide, is caused by Moraxella bovis, whose two indispensable virulence factors are:
options: Heat-stable enterotoxin and bundle-forming fimbriae
Capsular hyaluronic acid and neuraminidase
Lipooligosaccharide endotoxin and IgA1 protease
Type IV fimbriae and an RTX beta-hemolysin
explanation: Moraxella bovis requires Type IV fimbriae (specifically the Q-pilus / I-pilus phase variants) to adhere to corneal epithelial cells against tear flushing, and secretes a calcium-dependent pore-forming RTX cytotoxin/hemolysin (MbxA) that lyses corneal epithelium and bovine neutrophils.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In the classical biotyping of Brucella species, how do typical wild-type strains of Brucella abortus (Biovar 1) and Brucella melitensis (Biovar 1) differ in CO2 requirement, H2S production, and dye sensitivity (Thionin vs Basic Fuchsin at 1:50,000)?
options: B. abortus requires CO2, produces H2S, and is inhibited by Thionin; B. melitensis needs no CO2, produces no H2S, and grows in both dyes
Both species require 10% CO2, produce abundant H2S, and are completely inhibited by both Thionin and Basic Fuchsin
B. abortus needs no CO2, produces no H2S, and grows in both dyes; B. melitensis requires CO2, produces H2S, and is inhibited by Basic Fuchsin
B. abortus grows in Thionin but is inhibited by Basic Fuchsin; B. melitensis is inhibited by both Thionin and Basic Fuchsin
explanation: Classical differential table for Brucella: B. abortus (Biovar 1) requires 5–10% CO2 on primary isolation, produces H2S (blackening lead acetate strips), is inhibited by Thionin, and grows in Basic Fuchsin. B. melitensis requires no CO2, produces no H2S, and grows in the presence of both Thionin and Basic Fuchsin (whereas B. suis grows in Thionin and is inhibited by Basic Fuchsin).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Why does vaccination of cattle with the Brucella abortus 'RB51' vaccine strain NOT cause false-positive reactions on standard smooth-lipopolysaccharide serological tests (such as RBPT, STAT, and indirect ELISA), unlike the classical 'Strain 19' vaccine?
options: RB51 is a recombinant subunit vaccine containing only purified outer membrane protein Omp25
RB51 is a stable rough mutant lacking the immunodominant LPS O-polysaccharide chain
RB51 is administered exclusively via the intranasal route and induces only secretory IgA in tears
RB51 is heat-killed and adjuvanted with aluminum hydroxide, preventing IgG1 class switching
explanation: Brucella abortus Strain RB51 is a rifampicin-resistant, stable rough mutant bearing an IS711 insertion in the wboA glycosyltransferase gene. Because it lacks the smooth LPS O-antigen chain recognized by RBPT, STAT, and smooth-LPS ELISAs, vaccinated cattle remain seronegative on routine surveillance tests (enabling DIVA).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Which naturally rough Brucella species causes contagious epididymitis, tunica vaginalis adhesions, and sperm granulomas in rams (and sporadic placentitis in ewes) without possessing zoonotic potential for humans?
options: Brucella melitensis
Brucella suis
Brucella ovis
Brucella neotomae
explanation: Brucella ovis and Brucella canis are the two classical Brucella species that are naturally rough (lacking the LPS O-side chain) in their virulent wild-type state. B. ovis causes ovine contagious epididymitis in rams, requires 5–10% CO2, is non-urease producing, and is non-zoonotic.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Francisella tularensis, the causative agent of Tularemia ('rabbit fever') in lagomorphs, rodents, cats, and sheep, is a minute, fastidious Gram-negative coccobacillus that strictly requires supplementation of blood agar with which amino acid?
options: L-Tryptophan
D-Glutamic acid
Meso-diaminopimelic acid
L-Cysteine (or cystine)
explanation: Francisella tularensis is an obligate aerobic, facultative intracellular pathogen that cannot synthesize sulfhydryl compounds and requires media enriched with L-cysteine or cystine (such as Francis's glucose-cystine blood agar or Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract [BCYE] with cysteine).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Chromobacterium violaceum, an environmental water and soil bacterium that causes fatal pyogranulomatous pneumonia and hepatic abscesses in swine, cattle, and dogs in tropical regions, is immediately recognized in culture by producing:
options: A water-soluble blue-green phenazine pigment called pyocyanin
A fluorescent yellow-green siderophore pigment called pyoverdine
An insoluble deep violet-purple pigment called violacein
A brick-red prodigiosin pigment synthesized only at 25°C
explanation: Chromobacterium violaceum is a facultative anaerobic, motile Gram-negative rod that synthesizes violacein—an ethanol-soluble, water-insoluble deep violet tryptophan derivative with antioxidant and antimicrobial properties.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In diagnostic veterinary microbiology, Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis (the obligate venereal agent of bovine infertility) is differentiated biochemically from Campylobacter fetus subsp. fetus (cause of sporadic ovine and bovine abortion) based on its:
options: Inability to grow in media containing 1% Glycine
Strict requirement for 20% atmospheric oxygen and absence of catalase
Ability to grow rapidly at 42°C and hydrolyze sodium hippurate
Production of abundant urease and resistance to nalidixic acid
explanation: Both subspecies of Campylobacter fetus grow at 25°C and 37°C (but not 42°C) and are catalase-positive; however, C. fetus subsp. venerealis is intolerant of 1% glycine (no growth) and does not produce H2S in cysteine medium, whereas C. fetus subsp. fetus grows in 1% glycine.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Which thermophilic Campylobacter species grows optimally at 42°C to 43°C and is differentiated from Campylobacter coli in food safety and veterinary laboratories by its positive 'Hippurate Hydrolysis Test' (forming a deep purple color with ninhydrin)?
options: Campylobacter hyointestinalis
Campylobacter jejuni
Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis
Campylobacter sputorum biovar bubulus
explanation: Campylobacter jejuni is a thermophilic campylobacter (growing optimally at 42°C) and is the only major veterinary/zoonotic Campylobacter species that possesses the hipO gene encoding hippuricase, which hydrolyzes sodium hippurate into benzoic acid and glycine (detected with ninhydrin).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In Leptospira epidemiology, cattle serve as the natural maintenance (reservoir) host—characterized by chronic renal colonization, mild clinical signs, and persistent reproductive failure/milk drop syndrome—for which specific serovar?
options: Leptospira interrogans serovar Pomona
Leptospira interrogans serovar Icterohaemorrhagiae
Leptospira borgpetersenii
Leptospira interrogans serovar Canicola
explanation: Each Leptospira serovar is adapted to a specific maintenance reservoir host: Hardjo in cattle, Pomona and Tarassovi in swine, Canicola in dogs, Icterohaemorrhagiae and Copenhageni in rats, and Bratislava in horses and pigs.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: When Leptospira interrogans is inoculated into semi-solid Fletcher's or EMJH medium (containing 0.1–0.2% agar), growth characteristically appears 0.5 to 1.5 cm below the surface of the medium as a dense translucent disc known as:
options: The bottle-brush zone
Dinger's ring
Pfeiffer's phenomenon
The stalactite festoon
explanation: In semi-solid leptospiral media (Fletcher's or semi-solid EMJH), leptospires migrate to their optimal oxygen tension slightly below the meniscus, forming a well-defined flat horizontal band of turbidity called Dinger's ring (or Dinger's disk).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: How are non-pathogenic, free-living water saprophytes (Leptospira biflexa) differentiated in the laboratory from pathogenic strains (Leptospira interrogans)?
options: L. biflexa grows at 13°C
L. biflexa lacks periplasmic endoflagella and is strongly Gram-positive
L. biflexa fails to grow below 37°C and is lysed by 1% bile salts
L. biflexa requires Mycobactin J and 10% carbon dioxide for growth
explanation: Saprophytic Leptospira biflexa can replicate at low temperatures (13°C), grows in the presence of the purine analog 8-azaguanine (225 ug/mL), and converts to spherical bodies in 1 M NaCl, whereas pathogenic L. interrogans cannot grow at 13°C and is inhibited by 8-azaguanine.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Avian Spirochetosis—an acute fatal septicemic disease of chickens, turkeys, and ducks characterized by high fever, greenish diarrhea, paresis, and mottled enlarged spleen—is caused by Borrelia anserina and transmitted biologically by:
options: The biting midge Culicoides imicola
The hard prostriate deer tick Ixodes scapularis
The poultry red mite Dermanyssus gallinae
The soft argasid fowl tick Argas persicus
explanation: Borrelia anserina causes Avian Spirochetosis and is biologically transmitted (with transovarial and transstadial transmission) by the cosmopolitan soft fowl tick Argas persicus.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: While Brachyspira hyodysenteriae causes severe mucohemorrhagic Swine Dysentery, which weakly beta-hemolytic, hippurate-positive spirochete attaches by one pole to colonic enterocytes ('false brush border') to cause milder Porcine Intestinal Spirochetosis?
options: Treponema paraluiscuniculi
Leptospira interrogans serovar Pomona
Brachyspira suanatina
Brachyspira pilosicoli
explanation: Brachyspira pilosicoli is weakly beta-hemolytic on trypticase soy blood agar (unlike strongly beta-hemolytic, indole-positive B. hyodysenteriae), hydrolyzes hippurate, and causes Porcine Colonic Spirochetosis ('gray cement-like diarrhea') in grower pigs.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In poultry mycoplasmosis, how is Mycoplasma synoviae (the agent of infectious synovitis and airsacculitis) nutritionally distinguished from Mycoplasma gallisepticum during primary isolation on Frey's or PPLO medium?
options: Mycoplasma synoviae requires Mycobactin J and sodium pyruvate at pH 5.5
Mycoplasma synoviae is an obligate anaerobe that is killed by 5% carbon dioxide
Mycoplasma synoviae strictly requires supplementation with beta-NAD
Mycoplasma synoviae grows rapidly on nutrient agar without serum or cholesterol
explanation: Mycoplasma synoviae is fastidious and strictly requires reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (beta-NAD, 0.01%) and cysteine hydrochloride for in vitro growth on Frey's medium, whereas Mycoplasma gallisepticum grows without exogenous NAD.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Which specialized staining procedure is used to examine intact Mycoplasma colonies directly on agar blocks, staining the dense central core dark royal blue and the peripheral surface zone light blue without decolorization?
options: Dienes stain
Seller's basic fuchsin and methylene blue stain
Stamp's modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain
Schaeffer-Fulton malachite green stain
explanation: Dienes stain (an alcoholic/aqueous solution of methylene blue, azure II, maltose, and sodium carbonate) is applied to a coverslip placed directly over Mycoplasma colonies on agar. Live Mycoplasma colonies stay stained two-tone blue (dense dark blue center, light blue periphery), whereas bacterial L-forms or artifacts often reduce/decolorize the dye.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Mycoplasma haemofelis (formerly Haemobartonella felis) and Mycoplasma suis (formerly Eperythrozoon suis) belong to the 'Hemotropic Mycoplasmas' (hemoplasmas), which are characterized by:
options: Synthesizing a thick peptidoglycan cell wall that renders them susceptible to penicillin G
Attaching epicellularly to the outer surface of host erythrocytes
Multiplying exclusively inside the nucleus of circulating polymorphonuclear neutrophils
Growing abundantly on MacConkey agar into bright pink mucoid colonies within 18 hours
explanation: Hemotropic mycoplasmas (hemoplasmas) are wall-less epicellular bacteria that adhere tightly to indentations on the plasma membrane of host erythrocytes (inducing immune-mediated hemolytic anemia), have never been cultivated in vitro on cell-free media, and are treated with tetracyclines (doxycycline/oxytetracycline).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Coxiella burnetii displays 'Phase Variation' analogous to smooth-rough LPS variation in Enterobacteriaceae. In the serodiagnosis of human and ruminant Q Fever, what is the clinical significance of Phase I vs Phase II antibodies?
options: Phase II antibodies are restricted to horses, whereas Phase I antibodies occur only in poultry
Phase I antibodies appear only after vaccination, whereas Phase II antibodies indicate absence of infection
Anti-Phase II antibodies predominate in acute Q fever, whereas high anti-Phase I IgG titers indicate chronic Q fever
Phase I organisms lack LPS and grow only in cell culture, whereas Phase II organisms have full-length LPS
explanation: Virulent Coxiella burnetii in animals possesses smooth full-length LPS (Phase I), which sterically masks surface proteins. Consequently, the host mounts an early antibody response against exposed surface proteins (Phase II antigen) during acute infection, whereas sustained high IgG titers against Phase I LPS antigen are diagnostic of chronic Q fever (e.g., endocarditis/placentitis).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: 'Heartwater' (Cowdriosis)—a high-mortality tick-borne disease of cattle, sheep, and goats in sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean characterized by hydropericardium, hydrothorax, and neurological paddling—is caused by Ehrlichia ruminantium and transmitted by:
options: Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus one-host cattle ticks
Hyalomma anatolicum two-host ticks
Ornithodoros moubata soft argasid ticks
Amblyomma ticks
explanation: Ehrlichia ruminantium (formerly Cowdria ruminantium) is transmitted biologically by three-host bont ticks of the genus Amblyomma (A. variegatum, A. hebraeum) and is diagnosed post-mortem by demonstrating purplish colonies (morulae) inside capillary endothelial cells in Giemsa-stained cerebral cortex squash smears.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: 'Salmon Poisoning Disease'—an acute, highly fatal hemorrhagic enteritis and generalized lymphadenopathy in dogs that consume raw salmonid fish in the Pacific Northwest—is caused by which intracellular rickettsial bacterium carried inside the trematode vector Nanophyetus salmincola?
options: Ehrlichia ewingii
Neorickettsia helminthoeca
Rickettsia rickettsii
Anaplasma phagocytophilum
explanation: Neorickettsia helminthoeca is an obligate intracellular endosymbiont of the digenean fluke Nanophyetus salmincola. When dogs eat raw salmon or trout containing encysted fluke metacercariae, the adult flukes attach to the canine intestinal mucosa and inoculate N. helminthoeca into macrophages.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Potomac Horse Fever (Equine Neorickettsiosis / Equine Monocytic Ehrlichiosis), characterized by acute fever, depression, profuse watery diarrhea, colic, and severe laminitis in horses near freshwater streams during summer, is caused by:
options: Neorickettsia risticii transmitted
Anaplasma marginale transmitted by Dermacentor variabilis
Ehrlichia canis transmitted by Rhipicephalus sanguineus
Coxiella burnetii transmitted by inhalation of desiccated placental aerosols
explanation: Neorickettsia risticii (formerly Ehrlichia risticii) infects equine blood monocytes and colonic crypt epithelial cells. Horses acquire infection by accidentally ingesting emergent aquatic insects (mayflies, caddisflies, damselflies) carrying metacercariae of freshwater snail trematodes (Acanthatrium/Lecithodendrium).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Enzootic Abortion of Ewes (EAE / Ovine Enzootic Abortion), a major cause of late-gestation abortion, stillbirth, and necrotizing placentitis with thickened leathery intercotyledonary membranes in sheep and goats, is caused by:
options: Coxiella burnetii
Chlamydia abortus
Listeria ivanovii
Campylobacter jejuni
explanation: Chlamydia abortus is the premier infectious cause of abortion in sheep and goats in Europe and North America. Ewes infected in one pregnancy often abort in the final 2–3 weeks of the subsequent gestation, shedding vast numbers of elementary bodies visible as red coccoid clusters on Stamp's or Gimenez stain.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In the 'Gimenez Staining' protocol for demonstrating intracellular Chlamydia abortus elementary bodies and Rickettsia species in impression smears, how do the organisms appear microscopically?
options: Jet-black spiral filaments against a golden-brown silver-impregnated background
Dark purple rods surrounded by an unstained halo against a yellow picric acid background
Apple-green fluorescent filaments against a black potassium permanganate background
Bright red intracellular coccobacilli against a bluish-green host cell background
explanation: In the Gimenez stain, carbol basic fuchsin buffered with sodium phosphate stains Chlamydia elementary bodies, Rickettsia, and Coxiella bright red, while 0.8% aqueous malachite green oxalate counterstains the background host cells and debris bluish-green.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Haalstra's method for isolating Dermatophilus congolensis from dry, crusty scabs of cattle with rain scald (streptothricosis) exploits which specific biological behavior of its infective zoospores?
options: Release of motile zoospores upon moistening in distilled water followed by positive chemotaxis toward 10% CO2 atmosphere
Resistance of mature endospores to heating at 80°C for 30 minutes in ethanol
Selective survival in 10% potassium hydroxide and 5% sodium hypochlorite
Psychrophilic replication in nutrient broth held at 4°C for 6 weeks
explanation: In Haalstra's technique, small fragments of crust are placed in sterile distilled water at room temperature for 3.5 hours to stimulate release of motile zoospores, then transferred to a candle jar (CO2-enriched atmosphere) for 15 minutes; zoospores swim chemotactically to the surface meniscus toward CO2 and are streaked onto blood agar.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Streptobacillus moniliformis, the etiological agent of Rat-Bite Fever (and Haverhill fever) in rodents and humans, is culturally and morphologically notable in microbiology because it:
options: Requires 42°C microaerophilic incubation and forms seagull-shaped rods
Is a strict obligate intracellular rickettsia transmitted by the rat flea Xenopsylla cheopis
Forms pleomorphic filamentous chains with bulbous yeast-like swellings
Produces a bright violet pigment and grows on MacConkey agar without serum
explanation: Streptobacillus moniliformis is a fastidious Gram-negative pleomorphic rod (requiring 20% serum, blood, or ascitic fluid) that forms long tangled filaments with spherical/fusiform bulbous swellings ('moniliform' / string of beads) and spontaneously gives rise to cell-wall-deficient L-phase colonies ('fried-egg' appearance).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Which fastidious, Gram-negative intra-erythrocytic and endotheliotropic bacterium is maintained in a chronic subclinical bacteremia in domestic cats, transmitted between cats by the cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis), and causes zoonotic 'Cat Scratch Disease' in humans?
options: Bartonella henselae
Francisella tularensis
Mycoplasma haemofelis
Pasteurella multocida subsp. multocida
explanation: Bartonella henselae resides inside feline erythrocytes and is transmitted among cats via infected flea feces (Ctenocephalides felis) inoculated by scratching; in humans, a cat scratch or bite causes regional lymphadenopathy ('Cat Scratch Disease') or bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised individuals.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: 'Summer Mastitis' in dry dairy cows and pregnant heifers pastured in wooded areas is a severe suppurative mastitis characterized by thick, foul-smelling greenish pus, transmitted mechanically by the sheep headfly (Hydrotaea irritans), and caused by a synergistic infection of:
options: Mycoplasma bovis and Nocardia asteroides
Trueperella pyogenes
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus agalactiae
Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Klebsiella pneumoniae
explanation: Summer mastitis is a classic polymicrobial synergistic infection in which Trueperella pyogenes (formerly Arcanobacterium/Corynebacterium pyogenes) combines with the strict anaerobe Peptoniphilus indolicus (and Fusobacterium necrophorum), transmitted to the teat orifice by the fly Hydrotaea irritans.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: How is Trueperella pyogenes culturally differentiated from beta-hemolytic Streptococci when isolated from bovine suppurative lesions or mastitis milk?
options: T. pyogenes forms large mucoid colonies within 6 hours and is resistant to bacitracin and penicillin
T. pyogenes is strongly catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, and grows on MacConkey agar
T. pyogenes is an obligate intracellular organism that grows only in yolk sacs of embryonated eggs
T. pyogenes is a pleomorphic Gram-positive diphtheroid that pits Loeffler's coagulated serum slopes
explanation: Trueperella pyogenes is a catalase-negative, pinpoint beta-hemolytic, pleomorphic Gram-positive rod (coryneform/actinomycete) whose colonies become visible at 48 hours, secrete the cholesterol-dependent cytolysin Pyolysin (PLO), and characteristically pit (liquefy) Loeffler's coagulated serum slants.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Ornithobacterium rhinotracheale (ORT) has emerged globally as a major respiratory pathogen of turkeys and broiler chickens, causing:
options: Hard nodular caseous granulomas ('yellow buttons') in the lungs and air sacs of newly hatched chicks
Acute watery white diarrhea with chalky urate pasting around the vent in 3-day-old chicks
Fibrinopurulent pneumonia
Diphtheritic pseudomembranes in the larynx and hemorrhagic tracheitis with intranuclear inclusions
explanation: Ornithobacterium rhinotracheale is a slow-growing, pleomorphic Gram-negative rod (family Weeksrellaceae) that causes contagious respiratory disease, growth retardation, osteitis/meningitis, and a pathognomonic thick, white-to-yellow 'yogurt-like' fibrinopurulent exudate in the air sacs of turkeys and broilers.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Avian Pathogenic Escherichia coli (APEC), the cause of avian colibacillosis (airsacculitis, fibrinous perihepatitis, pericarditis, salpingitis, and omphalitis), predominantly belongs to which three somatic (O) serogroups worldwide?
options: O8, O9, and O101
O1, O2, and O78
explanation: While O157/O111/O26 are enterohemorrhagic (STEC) and O138/O139/O141 cause porcine edema disease, Avian Pathogenic E. coli (APEC) strains causing systemic colisepticemia and polyserositis in poultry predominantly belong to serogroups O1, O2, and O78.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In sheep, Listeria ivanovii (formerly Listeria monocytogenes serovar 5) differs from Listeria monocytogenes in both its clinical spectrum and its hemolysis on sheep blood agar because L. ivanovii:
options: Grows only at 42°C and produces black colonies on Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar
Causes ovine abortion and enteritis and produces wide, bizonal beta-hemolytic zone with positive CAMP reaction with Rhodococcus equi
Is an obligate anaerobe that fails to hydrolyze esculin and is CAMP-positive only with Staphylococcus aureus
Causes exclusively neural circling disease in adult rams and is completely non-hemolytic on blood agar
explanation: Listeria ivanovii is strongly beta-hemolytic on sheep blood agar (owing to ivanolysin O and sphingomyelinase C), gives a spade-shaped positive CAMP reaction with Rhodococcus equi (not S. aureus), ferments D-xylose (not L-rhamnose), and causes abortion in ewes without causing neural encephalitis.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: What is the definitive biochemical and cultural difference between Burkholderia pseudomallei (agent of Melioidosis) and Burkholderia mallei (agent of Glanders)?
options: B. pseudomallei is motile by polar flagella, grows at 42°C
B. pseudomallei is a Gram-positive branching filament that is partially acid-fast on Kinyoun stain
B. pseudomallei is non-motile, oxidase-negative, and fails to grow on MacConkey agar
B. pseudomallei is an obligate intracellular organism that requires L-cysteine and heated horse blood
explanation: Unlike Burkholderia mallei (an obligate mammalian pathogen that is non-motile due to deletion/frameshift in flagellar genes and grows poorly on selective media), B. pseudomallei is an environmental saprophyte that is actively motile via polar tuft of flagella, grows at 42°C, is gentamicin/polymyxin-resistant, and forms dry wrinkled purple colonies on Ashdown's agar.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In dogs and pigs, Bordetella bronchiseptica (a primary agent of Canine Infectious Respiratory Disease Complex / 'Kennel Cough' and non-progressive porcine atrophic rhinitis) is biochemically characterized as a Gram-negative coccobacillus that is:
options: Obligately anaerobic, H2S-positive on TSI agar, and indole-positive
Non-motile, lactose-fermenting, urease-negative, and oxidase-negative
Microaerophilic, darting-motile by a single polar flagellum, and hippurate-positive
Rapidly urease-positive
explanation: Unlike Bordetella pertussis (which is non-motile, urease-negative, and citrate-negative), Bordetella bronchiseptica is motile via peritrichous flagella, grows on MacConkey agar (non-lactose fermenter), is oxidase-positive, citrate-positive, and rapidly hydrolyzes urea within 4 hours.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: Anaplasma phagocytophilum (formerly Ehrlichia phagocytophila / Ehrlichia equi), the tick-borne agent of 'Tick-Borne Fever' in sheep and cattle and Granulocytic Anaplasmosis in horses and dogs, forms intracytoplasmic morulae predominantly inside:
options: Granulocytes (primarily neutrophils and eosinophils)
Mature circulating erythrocytes (at the extreme cell margin)
Circulating blood platelets (thrombocytes)
Cerebral capillary vascular endothelial cells
explanation: Whereas Anaplasma marginale/centrale infect erythrocytes, Anaplasma platys infects platelets, and Ehrlichia canis/chaffeensis infect monocytes, Anaplasma phagocytophilum (and Ehrlichia ewingii) selectively infects granulocytes (neutrophils and eosinophils), causing severe neutropenia and immunosuppression ('tick-borne fever' in lambs).

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: In guinea pigs, cervical lymphadenitis ('Lumps') characterized by massive abscessation of the submandibular and cervical lymph nodes is classically caused by which beta-hemolytic Lancefield Group C streptococcus?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus suis serotype 2
Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus
Streptococcus agalactiae
explanation: Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus (Lancefield Group C, which ferments sorbitol and lactose unlike S. equi subsp. equi) is a normal mucosal commensal of cavies that invades Oral abrasions from coarse feed to cause classic Cervical Lymphadenitis ('Lumps') in guinea pigs, as well as Opportunistic endometritis and pneumonia in horses.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: How is Streptococcus equi subsp. equi (the obligate agent of equine Strangles) biochemically differentiated from the closely related opportunist Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus (both in Lancefield Group C)?
options: S. equi subsp. equi ferments both sorbitol and lactose; S. zooepidemicus ferments neither
S. equi subsp. equi fails to ferment sorbitol and lactose
S. equi subsp. equi is strongly catalase-positive and grows in 6.5% NaCl broth
S. equi subsp. equi hydrolyzes esculin and hippurate, whereas S. zooepidemicus is negative for both
explanation: Sugar fermentation is the gold-standard phenotypic test to distinguish the Lancefield Group C equine streptococci: Streptococcus equi subsp. equi is negative for sorbitol, lactose, and trehalose fermentation, whereas S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus ferments both sorbitol and lactose.

topic: Systematic Bacteriology (Gram +ve, Gram -ve, Acid-Fast, Spirochetes & Mycoplasma)
questionText: The antiphagocytic cell-wall protein of Streptococcus equi subsp. equi that binds host fibrinogen and complement factor H, induces protective mucosal immunity, and serves as the basis for serotyping and subunit strangles vaccines is:
options: Protein A (Spa)
VapA lipoprotein
Internalin A (InlA)
SeM protein
explanation: Streptococcus equi subsp. equi expresses a surface-anchored M-like fibrillar protein designated SeM, which binds fibrinogen and IgG-Fc to block C3b deposition and neutrophil phagocytosis; SeM is the principal protective immunogen in equine strangles.

questionText: The rigid cell wall of true pathogenic fungi (Eumycota) is structurally composed of chitin and beta-glucans, while their plasma membrane contains which principal sterol in place of mammalian cholesterol?
options: Stigmasterol (targeted by echinocandins)
Lanosterol (targeted by griseofulvin)
Ergosterol
Hopanoids (targeted by polymyxin E)
explanation: True fungi contain chitin (beta-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine) and beta-1,3/1,6-D-glucans in their cell wall, and utilize Ergosterol as the primary sterol maintaining plasma membrane fluidity and integrity.

questionText: Polyene macrolide antifungal drugs (such as Amphotericin B, Nystatin, and Natamycin) exert their rapid fungicidal action by:
options: Binding directly to membrane ergosterol to form transmembrane ion-leaking pores
Disrupting mitotic spindle microtubules by binding polymerized fungal tubulin
Non-competitively inhibiting beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase in the fungal cell wall
Inhibiting cytochrome P450 14-alpha-sterol demethylase in the endoplasmic reticulum
explanation: Polyene antifungals (Amphotericin B, Nystatin, Natamycin) are amphipathic molecules that bind directly to ergosterol in the fungal plasma membrane, assembling into transmembrane hydrophilic pores that cause lethal leakage of intracellular K+ and Mg2+.

questionText: Azole antifungal agents (such as Itraconazole, Fluconazole, Ketoconazole, and Enilconazole) inhibit fungal growth by blocking the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol via inhibition of which enzyme?
options: Squalene epoxidase (encoded by ERG1)
Beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase (encoded by FKS1)
Thymidylate synthase and cytosine deaminase
Cytochrome P450-dependent 14-alpha-sterol demethylase
explanation: Imidazoles (ketoconazole, enilconazole, miconazole) and triazoles (itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole) bind the heme iron of fungal cytochrome P450 14-alpha-sterol demethylase (CYP51), depleting ergosterol and accumulating toxic 14-alpha-methyl sterols.

questionText: The allylamine antifungal drug Terbinafine, widely used for treating dermatophytosis, is fungicidal against dermatophytes because it selectively inhibits which early enzyme in sterol biosynthesis, causing toxic intracellular accumulation of squalene?
options: HMG-CoA reductase
Squalene epoxidase (ERG1)
14-alpha-sterol demethylase (CYP51A1)
Chitin synthase-3 (CHS3)
explanation: Allylamines (terbinafine, naftifine) non-competitively inhibit fungal squalene epoxidase (squalene monooxygenase), blocking the conversion of squalene to squalene-2,3-epoxide; the resulting intracellular accumulation of squalene is directly fungicidal.

questionText: Echinocandin antifungals (such as Caspofungin and Micafungin) are referred to as 'fungal penicillins' because they inhibit the synthesis of which essential fungal cell wall component?
options: Ergosterol (by inhibiting delta-14-sterol reductase)
Beta-(1,3)-D-glucan (by inhibiting beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase)
Mannoproteins (by inhibiting dolichol phosphate mannosyltransferase)
Chitin polymers (by inhibiting UDP-N-acetylglucosamine transferase)
explanation: Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) are cyclic lipopeptides that non-competitively inhibit the catalytic subunit Fks1p of beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, causing osmotic lysis of Candida and hyphal tip lysis of Aspergillus.

questionText: Griseofulvin, an oral fungistatic antibiotic derived from Penicillium griseofulvum used solely for systemic treatment of dermatophytosis, acts intracellularly by:
options: Binding to polymerized tubulin to disrupt the fungal mitotic spindle
Inhibiting fungal dihydrofolate reductase and purine biosynthesis
Chelation of ferric iron required by fungal catalase and peroxidase
Forming hydrophilic pores across the nuclear envelope of arthrospores
explanation: Griseofulvin is absorbed better with a fatty meal, deposits in newly forming keratin precursor cells of skin, hair, and claws, and binds fungal microtubule proteins (tubulin) to arrest fungal mitosis in metaphase. Because it disrupts microtubules, it is teratogenic in pregnant queens (causing cleft palate and cyclopia).

questionText: Flucytosine (5-Fluorocytosine, 5-FC) exhibits selective toxicity against pathogenic yeasts (Candida and Cryptococcus) while sparing mammalian host cells because mammalian cells lack which enzyme that converts 5-FC into 5-fluorouracil?
options: Xanthine oxidase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Cytosine deaminase
explanation: Flucytosine enters fungal cells via cytosine permease and is deaminated by fungal cytosine deaminase (an enzyme absent in mammalian cells) into 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), which is converted into 5-FdUMP (inhibiting thymidylate synthase/DNA synthesis) and 5-FUTP (disrupting RNA processing).

questionText: Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA), the universal primary culture medium for veterinary fungi, suppresses competing bacterial growth primarily by utilizing:
options: Crystal violet, potassium tellurite, and thallous acetate at pH 7.4
Malachite green and egg albumin inspissated at 85°C
High dextrose concentration (4%) and an acidic pH of 5.6
7.5% sodium chloride and 0.5% bile salts at an alkaline pH of 8.5
explanation: Formulated by Raymond Sabouraud in 1892, standard Sabouraud Dextrose Agar contains 4% dextrose (glucose) and 1% peptone adjusted to an acidic pH of 5.6, which inhibits most bacteria; for contaminated clinical skins/hairs, chloramphenicol (or gentamicin) and cycloheximide (actidione) are added.

questionText: On Dermatophyte Test Medium (DTM)—which contains cycloheximide, gentamicin, chlortetracycline, and Phenol Red indicator—pathogenic dermatophytes (Microsporum and Trichophyton) are presumptively identified within 7–14 days because they:
options: Rapidly ferment glucose into lactic acid, turning the medium from bright red to lemon yellow
Synthesize melanin from caffeic acid, turning the fungal colony dark brown
Reduce sodium thiosulfate to hydrogen sulfide, turning the agar base jet-black
Preferentially catabolize peptone proteins first, releasing alkaline metabolites
explanation: On DTM, pathogenic dermatophytes preferentially utilize nitrogenous peptones before carbohydrates, producing alkaline ammonium metabolites that raise the pH and turn the phenol red indicator from yellow (acidic) to bright red simultaneously with white/buff fluffy colony growth.

questionText: In the standard 'Lactophenol Cotton Blue' (LPCB) mounting fluid used for microscopic identification of fungal mycelia and conidia, what are the specific functions of Lactic acid, Phenol, and Cotton blue (Aniline blue)?
options: Lactic acid dissolves chitin; Phenol induces sporulation; Cotton blue stains lipid granules
Lactic acid preserves fungal structures; Phenol kills the fungus; Cotton blue stains chitin
Lactic acid kills the fungus; Phenol stains ergosterol; Cotton blue prevents drying
Lactic acid fixes nuclear chromatin; Phenol buffers pH to 8.0; Cotton blue quenches fluorescence
explanation: In LPCB: Lactic acid acts as a clearing and preserving agent that maintains intact fungal morphology; Phenol acts as a fungicide to kill live infectious spores; Glycerol prevents desiccation; and Cotton Blue (methyl blue/aniline blue) stains the chitinous cell wall deep blue.

questionText: Which two specialized histopathological stains are routinely employed to visualize fungal hyphae and yeasts in formalin-fixed tissue sections, staining fungal cell walls bright magenta-red and brown-black, respectively?
options: Periodic Acid-Schiff stain and Gomori Methenamine Silver stain
Congo red amyloid stain and Sudan Black B lipid stain
Masson's trichrome stain and Prussian blue stain
Ziehl-Neelsen stain and Albert's toluidine blue stain
explanation: Periodic acid oxidizes 1,2-glycol groups in fungal cell wall polysaccharides (glucans/mannans) into aldehydes that react with Schiff's leucofuchsin to stain fungi bright magenta (PAS), while chromic acid oxidation and methenamine-silver nitrate reduction (GMS) stain fungal walls sharp black.

questionText: When canine or feline ringworm lesions caused by Microsporum canis are examined in a darkened room under a Wood's Lamp (filtered ultraviolet light at 365 nm), infected hairs emit a bright apple-green fluorescence due to:
options: Melanin and aflatoxin B1 synthesized by saprophytic mycelia
Ergosterol peroxides accumulated within the fungal plasma membrane
Water-soluble pteridine pigment metabolite produced in actively growing invaded hair shafts
Calcium dipicolinate chelated inside thick-walled macroconidia
explanation: Wood's lamp (UV-A light at 365 nm filtered through cobalt/nickel glass) excites a tryptophan-derived pteridine metabolite produced ONLY when Microsporum canis actively invades growing hair shafts in vivo; in vitro colonies on agar do not fluoresce similarly.

questionText: Which geophilic (soil-inhabiting) dermatophyte frequently causes focal crusty ringworm lesions on the muzzle and legs of dogs and horses, does NOT fluoresce under Wood's lamp, and forms cinnamon-buff powdery colonies with thin-walled, rough, 4-to-6-celled ellipsoidal macroconidia?
options: Epidermophyton floccosum (anthropophilic club-shaped macroconidia)
Microsporum canis (zoophilic spindle-shaped 6-to-15-celled macroconidia)
Microsporum gypseum (reclassified as Nannizzia gypsea)
Trichophyton verrucosum (zoophilic cattle dermatophyte)
explanation: Microsporum gypseum (Nannizzia gypsea) is the classic geophilic dermatophyte acquired by dogs rooting/digging in soil; its colonies grow rapidly as flat cinnamon-tan suede-like powders producing abundant thin-walled, echinulate, boat/ellipsoid macroconidia with 4–6 cells and rounded ends.

questionText: What is the primary host-adapted dermatophyte responsible for porcine ringworm (characterized by centrifugally expanding, brown crusted skin lesions behind the ears and on the flanks of adult pigs) that produces distinctive small, pear-shaped 2-celled macroconidia?
options: Microsporum nanum
Trichophyton gallinae
Trichophyton equinum
Microsporum audouinii
explanation: Microsporum nanum is the specific dermatophyte of swine worldwide; microscopically on LPCB mounts, it is uniquely identified by numerous small, ovoid-to-pear-shaped (pyriform), thin-walled macroconidia divided into only two (occasionally three) cells.

questionText: Most classical strains of Trichophyton equinum, the premier cause of equine dermatophytosis ('Girth Itch' in horses), are nutritionally distinguished in Trichophyton Agar #1–#7 testing by their strict requirement for which vitamin?
options: L-Histidine (Trichophyton Agar #6)
Thiamine and Inositol (Trichophyton Agar #3)
Para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)
Nicotinic acid
explanation: Whereas Trichophyton verrucosum of cattle requires thiamine and inositol (T-agar #3 and #4) and grows better at 37°C, classical Trichophyton equinum var. equinum of horses has an absolute nutritional requirement for nicotinic acid (niacin, T-agar #5).

questionText: 'Avian Favus' ('White Comb'), a chronic dermatophytosis of chickens and turkeys characterized by chalky white, flour-like crusts on the comb and wattles that may spread to feathered skin, is caused by:
options: Macrorhabdus ornithogaster
Trichophyton gallinae
Aspergillus flavus
Candida albicans
explanation: Trichophyton gallinae (Lophophyton gallinae) is the zoophilic dermatophyte of poultry that causes Avian Favus ('White Comb') and produces a characteristic strawberry-red diffusible pigment on the reverse side of Sabouraud dextrose agar.

questionText: When Candida albicans is inoculated onto nutritionally poor Cornmeal Tween-80 Agar at 25°C (Dalmau plate technique under a coverslip), it is definitively identified by forming pseudohyphae bearing:
options: Large, round, thick-walled terminal Chlamydoconidia (chlamydospores)
Dichotomously branching septate hyphae with conidial heads and phialides
Barrel-shaped arthroconidia alternating with empty disjunctor cells
Spindle-shaped, rough-walled, 12-celled macroconidia with terminal knobs
explanation: In addition to forming true germ tubes without constriction in serum at 37°C within 2 hours (Reynolds-Braude phenomenon), Candida albicans (and C. dubliniensis) forms characteristic large, refractile, thick-walled spherical chlamydoconidia (chlamydospores) on Cornmeal Tween-80 agar.

questionText: On Niger Seed Agar (Guizotia abyssinica / Staib's birdseed agar) containing caffeic acid, Cryptococcus neoformans forms diagnostic dark brown-to-black colonies due to the activity of which virulence enzyme?
options: Keratinolytic serine protease, which digests stratum corneum proteins
Phenol oxidase, which synthesizes melanin from diphenolic substrates
Cytoplasmic urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonium carbonate
Extracellular phospholipase B
explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans and C. gattii are the only pathogenic yeasts that possess copper-dependent phenol oxidase (laccase), which converts diphenolic compounds (such as caffeic acid in birdseed/Niger seed agar or L-DOPA in brain tissue) into dark brown-black melanin pigment that protects the yeast from oxidative killing.

questionText: How does Malassezia pachydermatis—the peanut-shaped unipolar budding yeast causing canine otitis externa and seborrheic dermatitis—differ nutritionally from all other species in the genus Malassezia (such as M. furfur and M. globosa)?
options: It grows only at 42°C on media supplemented with pigeon droppings
It requires thiamine, inositol, and nicotinic acid for budding
It is only non-lipid-dependent species capable of growing on standard Sabouraud dextrose agar without olive oil
It is an obligate anaerobe that requires 10% hydrogen gas and cysteine
explanation: All human-associated Malassezia species (M. furfur, M. sympodialis, M. globosa) are obligately lipid-dependent (requiring long-chain C12–C24 fatty acids / olive oil overlay on Dixon's agar because they lack fatty acid synthase). Malassezia pachydermatis is uniquely non-lipid-dependent and grows readily on plain Sabouraud dextrose agar.

questionText: Sporothrix schenckii (and Sporothrix brasiliensis in cats) causes lymphocutaneous 'Rose Gardener's Disease' in horses, cats, and dogs. In histopathological sections and pus smears, its pleomorphic 'cigar-shaped' yeast cells are characteristically surrounded by:
options: A thick-walled spherule membrane enclosing hundreds of endospores
Double-contoured refractile walls with broad-based unipolar buds
A wide, unstained mucopolysaccharide capsule demonstrated by India ink
Star-like eosinophilic radiate Splendore-Hoeppli projections termed 'Asteroid Bodies'
explanation: Sporothrix schenckii is a thermally dimorphic fungus (delicate 'daisy-head' conidiophores at 25°C; pleomorphic elongated 'cigar-shaped' yeasts at 37°C). In host tissues, yeast cells are frequently encased in a stellate, brightly eosinophilic antigen-antibody complex halo (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) called an Asteroid Body.

questionText: In its saprophytic mycelial phase grown on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25°C, Histoplasma capsulatum produces which pathognomonic diagnostic conidial structure?
options: Multiseptate spindle-shaped macroconidia with a curved apical beak
Large and spherical
Uncoiled helical sporangiophores terminating in a dark columella and sporangium
Alternating barrel-shaped arthroconidia separated by empty disjunctor cells
explanation: While Histoplasma capsulatum exists in host tissues at 37°C as small (2–4 um) intracellular budding yeasts inside macrophages, its mold phase at 25°C produces diagnostic large (8–14 um), round, thick-walled 'tuberculate macroconidia' bearing spiky tuberculate projections.

questionText: 'Epizootic Lymphangitis' ('Pseudoglanders')—a chronic, contagious, ulcerating pyogranulomatous lymphangitis of the limbs, neck, and nostrils of horses, mules, and donkeys—is caused by:
options: Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum
Burkholderia mallei
Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis biovar equi
Coccidioides immitis
explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum (formerly Cryptococcus farciminosus) causes Epizootic Lymphangitis in equids, clinically mimicking cutaneous glanders ('farcy'). Giemsa or Gram-stained smears of pus reveal numerous oval, lemon-shaped, double-contoured yeast cells (2.5–4 um) both inside macrophages and extracellularly.

questionText: Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii (causative agents of 'Valley Fever' in dogs, horses, and camelids in arid regions) are dimorphic fungi that replicate inside host tissues at 37°C not by yeast budding, but by forming:
options: Elongated cigar-shaped blastoconidia surrounded by eosinophilic asteroid bodies
Narrow intracellular yeasts inside reticuloendothelial macrophages
Large, thick-walled 'Spherules'
Broad-based budding yeast cells with thick double-refractile walls
explanation: In desert soil (25°C), Coccidioides forms infectious barrel-shaped arthroconidia. Once inhaled into the lungs of dogs or horses (37°C), each arthroconidium rounds up into a giant multinucleated 'spherule' (20–80 um) whose cytoplasm undergoes progressive cleavage to release hundreds of endospores.

questionText: In histopathological tissue sections of cattle with mycotic rumenitis or placentitis, how are Zygomycetes of the order Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus, Lichtheimia/Absidia) morphologically differentiated from Aspergillus fumigatus?
options: Mucorales form pigmented brown septate hyphae and sclerotic Medlar bodies
Mucorales form exclusively budding yeasts and pseudohyphae without true mycelia
Mucorales form narrow (2–3 um) regularly septate hyphae with acute 45° dichotomous branching
Mucorales form broad, ribbon-like, pauciseptate hyphae with wide right-angle branching
explanation: Aspergillus species produce narrow (3–6 um), uniform, parallel-walled, regularly septate hyphae that branch dichotomously at acute 45° angles. In contrast, Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus, Lichtheimia) produce wide (10–25 um), irregular, collapsible ribbon-like, non-septate (pauciseptate) hyphae that branch erratically at 90° right angles and aggressively invade blood vessels.

questionText: In horses, 'Guttural Pouch Mycosis'—a life-threatening infection in which a fungal diphtheritic plaque grows on the roof of the medial compartment of the guttural pouch—frequently causes sudden death by eroding the wall of the:
options: Nasolacrimal duct and facial artery (causing submandibular hematoma)
Tracheal bifurcation and cranial vena cava (causing hemothorax)
Ethmoid turbinates and optic chiasm (causing acute blindness)
Internal carotid artery (causing fatal spontaneous epistaxis)
explanation: Equine guttural pouch mycosis (caused primarily by Aspergillus fumigatus and A. nidulans) forms a necrohemorrhagic mycotic plaque directly over the internal carotid artery (or external carotid/maxillary artery) and glossopharyngeal/vagus nerves (CN IX, X), leading to fatal arterial rupture (epistaxis), pharyngeal paralysis (dysphagia), and Horner's syndrome.

questionText: Pythium insidiosum—the etiological agent of 'Equine and Canine Pythiosis' ('Swamp Cancer', 'Leeches', or 'Bursattee') characterized by pruritic granulomatous cutaneous masses containing coral-like 'kunkers'—is resistant to standard azole and polyene antifungals because it is:
options: An acid-fast actinomycete whose cell wall is composed of mycolic acids and peptidoglycan
An aquatic Oomycete whose cell wall contains cellulose
An obligate intracellular microsporidian parasite that lacks mitochondria and peroxisomes
A cyanobacterium that synthesizes microcystin and saxitoxin in stagnant ponds
explanation: Pythium insidiosum is not a true fungus (Eumycota), but a fungus-like aquatic Oomycete (water mold). Because its cell wall contains beta-glucans and cellulose (not chitin) and its plasma membrane lacks ergosterol, ergosterol-targeting drugs (amphotericin B, itraconazole) are generally ineffective.

questionText: Prototheca zopfii (cause of incurable chronic granulomatous bovine mastitis) and Prototheca wickerhamii (cause of canine cutaneous and ocular protothecosis) are taxonomically classified as:
options: Achlorophyllous unicellular green algae that reproduce by endosporulation
Aquatic chytridiomycetes that infect amphibians and waterfowl
Thermophilic actinomycetes related to Dermatophilus
Dimorphic basidiomycetous yeasts related to Cryptococcus
explanation: Prototheca species are colorless (achlorophyllous) saprophytic mutant green microalgae (family Chlorellaceae) that lost their chloroplasts. In tissues and milk, they form oval-to-spherical sporangia (theca) that cleave internally into 2 to 16 daughter endospores (autospores) arranged in a 'morula' or 'Mercedes-Benz star' pattern.

questionText: Pneumocystis carinii (and Pneumocystis canis)—which causes fatal diffuse interstitial pneumonia with foamy eosinophilic alveolar casts in Arabian foals with SCID and immunodeficient dogs—is an atypical fungus that does NOT respond to amphotericin B or azoles and is instead treated with:
options: Ivermectin combined with praziquantel
Penicillin G combined with streptomycin
Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (Co-trimoxazole)
Griseofulvin combined with oral potassium iodide
explanation: Although ribosomal RNA phylogeny established that Pneumocystis is an atypical ascomycetous fungus, its plasma membrane contains cholesterol (scavenged from the host) rather than ergosterol, making polyenes and azoles useless. It is treated and prevented with Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (or pentamidine/atovaquone).

questionText: Encephalitozoon cuniculi, an obligate intracellular spore-forming microsporidian parasite closely related to fungi, infects rabbits via urinary spore ingestion and causes which classic clinical triad of lesions?
options: Hyperplastic biliary cirrhosis, cutaneous myxomatosis, and splenic infarction
Caseous bronchopneumonia, ulcerative typhlitis, and degenerative polymyositis
Granulomatous meningoencephalitis, chronic interstitial nephritis, and phacoclastic uveitis
Hemorrhagic tracheitis, fibrinous pericarditis, and hepatic coccidiosis
explanation: Encephalitozoon cuniculi extrudes a coiled polar tubule to inject its sporoplasm into host cells, showing a strong tropism for the brain (vestibular torticollis/wry neck), kidneys (pitted cortical scars), and the developing lens of the eye (anterior lens capsule rupture and phacoclastic uveitis).

questionText: Macrorhabdus ornithogaster (formerly known as 'Megabacteria' and now recognized as 'Avian Gastric Yeast') is a very large, Gram-positive, PAS-positive rod-shaped ascomycetous yeast that colonizes which specific anatomical site in budgerigars, canaries, and finches, causing 'Going Light Syndrome'?
options: Narrow isthmus between proventriculus and ventriculus
The parabronchi and abdominal air sacs
The cecal tonsils and cloacal bursa of Fabricius
The mucosal epithelium of the crop and cervical esophagus
explanation: Macrorhabdus ornithogaster is an elongated (20–90 um long) filamentous yeast that forms a dense palisading mat specifically in the koilin/mucus layer at the isthmus connecting the glandular proventriculus and muscular ventriculus, causing proventricular dilatation, regurgitation of undigested seeds, and chronic emaciation ('going light').

questionText: The four major naturally occurring Aflatoxins (B1, B2, G1, and G2) were named based on their thin-layer chromatography (TLC) mobility and the characteristic color of their fluorescence under long-wave ultraviolet light (365 nm):
options: Aflatoxins B1/B2 are produced by Bacillus, while Aflatoxins G1/G2 are produced by Geotrichum
Aflatoxins B1/B2 fluoresce Blood-red, while Aflatoxins G1/G2 fluoresce Golden-orange
Aflatoxins B1/B2 bind Bile acids, while Aflatoxins G1/G2 bind Glomerular capillaries
Aflatoxins B1/B2 fluoresce Blue, while Aflatoxins G1/G2 fluoresce Green
explanation: Aflatoxins B1 and B2 (cyclopentenone ring fused to the coumarin lactone) emit a bright Blue fluorescence under UV light (365 nm), whereas Aflatoxins G1 and G2 (six-membered lactone ring) emit a yellow-Green fluorescence. Aflatoxin M1 (hydroxylated metabolite of B1) was named because it was isolated from Milk.

questionText: In hepatocarcinogenesis induced by Aflatoxin B1, hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes convert AFB1 into the reactive AFB1-8,9-exo-epoxide, which covalently binds the N7 position of guanine in DNA and characteristically induces which signature mutation in the p53 tumor suppressor gene?
options: An A-to-G transition at codon 12 of the ras proto-oncogene
A G-to-T transversion
Chromosomal translocation t(8;14) activating c-myc
A frameshift deletion of 3 base pairs at codon 508
explanation: The AFB1-8,9-epoxide forms a bulky AFB1-N7-guanine DNA adduct that undergoes depurination or ring opening to form a stable formamidopyrimidine (AFB1-FAPY) lesion, driving a signature G:C to T:A transversion specifically at codon 249 of the p53 tumor suppressor gene.

questionText: Which feed additive class is most widely and effectively incorporated into poultry and livestock diets to selectively adsorb Aflatoxins via their planar beta-dicarbonyl ring system in the gastrointestinal tract and prevent systemic bioavailability?
options: Hydrated Sodium Calcium Aluminosilicate
Propionic acid and calcium propionate mold inhibitors
Ethoxyquin and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) synthetic lipid antioxidants
Zinc bacitracin and monensin sodium ionophore coccidiostats
explanation: Phyllosilicate clays—specifically Hydrated Sodium Calcium Aluminosilicate (HSCAS), bentonites, and montmorillonite smectites—intercalate and chelate the planar beta-dicarbonyl moiety of Aflatoxin B1 with high affinity in the gut lumen, reducing hepatic uptake and milk Aflatoxin M1 excretion.

questionText: Classic 'Ergotism' in cattle and swine results from ingestion of cereal grains (especially rye, triticale, and barley) whose ovaries have been replaced by hard, dark purple-black banana-shaped fungal sclerotia of:
options: Penicillium verrucosum
Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae)
Aspergillus parasiticus
Claviceps purpurea
explanation: Claviceps purpurea infects the florets of rye and other small grains, replacing the developing seed kernel with a dense, dark purple-black overwintering mycelial mass called a sclerotium ('ergot' / 'cock's spur') rich in ergopeptine alkaloids (ergotamine, ergocristine, ergometrine).

questionText: Ergopeptine alkaloids (such as ergotamine from Claviceps purpurea and ergovaline from tall fescue endophytes) produce two major pharmacological syndromes in livestock: dry gangrene of the extremities (hooves, tail, ears) and agalactia in sows and mares. Through which two receptor mechanisms do these occur?
options: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor blockade (gangrene) and GABA-A chloride channel opening (agalactia)
Muscarinic M3 receptor agonism (gangrene) and beta-2 adrenergic blockade (agalactia)
Alpha-adrenergic
Histamine H1 receptor activation (gangrene) and oxytocin receptor antagonism (agalactia)
explanation: Ergot alkaloids contain a tetracyclic ergoline ring structurally homologous to norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine. Agonism at vascular alpha-adrenergic and 5-HT2A receptors causes intense arteriolar vasoconstriction and ischemic dry gangrene, while agonism at lactotroph Dopamine D2 receptors suppresses prolactin secretion, causing agalactia.

questionText: 'Fescue Foot', 'Summer Slump', and prolonged gestation/agalactia with thickened 'red bag' placentas in broodmares are caused by grazing Tall Fescue (Festuca arundinacea) infected with which mutualistic seed-borne endophytic fungus?
options: Rhizoctonia leguminicola
Epichloë coenophiala
Pithomyces chartarum
Stachybotrys chartarum
explanation: Epichloë coenophiala (formerly Neotyphodium coenophialum / Acremonium coenophialum) grows intercellularly inside tall fescue grass and is transmitted vertically through seeds, synthesizing the vasoconstrictive and dopaminergic ergopeptine alkaloid ergovaline.

questionText: What is the specific pharmacological antidote administered orally to late-pregnant broodmares grazing endophyte-infected tall fescue to block Dopamine D2 receptors on pituitary lactotrophs, restore prolactin secretion, and prevent agalactia without crossing the blood-brain barrier?
options: Yohimbine hydrochloride
Bromocriptine mesylate
Atropine sulfate
Domperidone
explanation: Domperidone is a peripheral selective Dopamine D2 receptor antagonist that competitively blocks ergovaline at the anterior pituitary lactotrophs, restoring normal periparturient prolactin surges, mammary development, and normal gestation length in mares.

questionText: 'Facial Eczema' (Pithomycotoxicosis) in grazing sheep, goats, and dairy cattle in New Zealand, Australia, and South Africa is a severe secondary (hepatogenous) photosensitization caused by ingestion of pasture litter containing spores of Pithomyces chartarum, which produce the hepatotoxin:
options: Fumonisin B1
Penitrem A
Sporidesmin
Phomopsin A
explanation: Pithomyces chartarum spores contain the epipolythiodioxopiperazine mycotoxin Sporidesmin, which undergoes redox cycling in bile canaliculi to generate superoxide radicals, causing necrotizing obliterative cholangiohepatitis. The damaged liver cannot excrete phylloerythrin (the photodynamic breakdown product of chlorophyll), leading to severe facial and ear photosensitization.

questionText: In hepatogenous photosensitization caused by Sporidesmin ('Facial Eczema') or Lantana camara toxicity in ruminants, what is the exact photodynamic pigment derived from ruminal microbial degradation of dietary chlorophyll that accumulates in systemic blood and skin when biliary excretion is obstructed?
options: Phylloerythrin
Hypericin (primary photosensitizing naphthodianthrone pigment)
Uroporphyrin I (congenital erythropoietic porphyria pigment)
Conjugated bilirubin diglucuronide
explanation: In the rumen, anaerobic bacteria convert dietary chlorophyll into the fluorescent porphyrin derivative Phylloerythrin. A healthy liver extracts phylloerythrin from portal blood and excretes it harmlessly into bile; when sporidesmin damages bile ducts, phylloerythrin enters peripheral skin capillaries and absorbs UV light, generating singlet oxygen.

questionText: 'Slobbers Syndrome'—characterized by profuse ptyalism (salivation), lacrimation, diarrhea, and bloat in horses and cattle consuming red clover (Trifolium pratense) hay infected with the black-patch fungus Rhizoctonia leguminicola—is caused by which parasympathomimetic mycotoxin?
options: Swainsonine (locoweed alpha-mannosidase inhibitor)
Slaframine
Satratoxin H (macrocyclic trichothecene)
Lolitrem B (indole-diterpene tremorgen)
explanation: Rhizoctonia leguminicola (Slafractonia leguminicola, causing 'black patch disease' on red clover) synthesizes the indolizidine alkaloid Slaframine, which is oxidized by hepatic microsomal flavoprotein monooxygenases into a ketoimine that directly stimulates muscarinic acetylcholine (M3) receptors on salivary glands and pancreas (treatable with atropine).

questionText: Cattle fed moldy, damaged sweet potatoes (Ipomoea batatas) colonized by the fungus Fusarium solani develop acute, fatal 'Atypical Interstitial Pneumonia' (pulmonary edema and emphysema) because the fungus metabolizes sweet potato phytoalexins into which pneumotoxic furanoterpenoid?
options: Fumonisin B1 (inhibitor of sphinganine N-acyltransferase)
4-Ipomeanol (bioactivated by pulmonary Clara/club cell CYP450 enzymes)
Dicoumarol (vitamin K epoxide reductase antagonist from moldy sweet clover)
3-Methylindole (produced from L-tryptophan by ruminal Lactobacillus)
explanation: When sweet potatoes are injured and infected by Fusarium solani, stress metabolites are converted into 4-Ipomeanol. After ingestion by cattle, 4-ipomeanol is selectively bioactivated by cytochrome P450 (CYP4B1) inside non-ciliated bronchiolar epithelial (Clara/club) cells into a reactive dialdehyde that destroys Type I pneumocytes.

questionText: 'Lupinosis' in sheep and cattle grazing lupin stubbles colonized by the fungus Diaporthe toxica (formerly Phomopsis leptostromiformis) is a severe mycotoxic hepatosis characterized histologically by arrest of hepatocytes in mitotic metaphase due to which mycotoxins?
options: Aflatoxins B1 and G1 (which alkylate guanine bases in DNA)
Oosporein and Citrinin (which uncouple renal mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation)
Phomopsins (hexapeptide mycotoxins
Rubratoxins A and B (which inhibit protein phosphatase 2A)
explanation: Diaporthe toxica (Phomopsis leptostromiformis) growing on lupin stalks produces cyclic hexapeptide mycotoxins called Phomopsins (Phomopsin A). Phomopsins bind tightly to tubulin, preventing microtubule polymerization and arresting dividing hepatocytes in abnormal C-mitosis (metaphase arrest), leading to fatty liver, icterus, andlupinosis.

questionText: 'Perennial Ryegrass Staggers' in sheep, cattle, horses, and alpacas—characterized by fine head tremors, head nodding, stiff-legged hopping ataxia, and collapse when excited—is caused by grazing Lolium perenne infected with the endophyte Epichloë festucae var. lolii, which synthesizes:
options: Swainsonine (an indolizidine alkaloid inhibiting lysosomal alpha-mannosidase)
Corynetoxins (tunicamycin-like glycolipid inhibitors from Rathayibacter toxicus)
Ergovaline (a vasoconstrictive ergopeptine alkaloid)
Lolitrem B (a potent indole-diterpene tremorgenic neurotoxin)
explanation: While the tall fescue endophyte (Epichloë coenophiala) produces ergovaline (fescue foot), the perennial ryegrass endophyte (Epichloë festucae var. lolii) produces the indole-diterpene neurotoxin Lolitrem B, which blocks large-conductance calcium-activated potassium (BK) channels in the cerebellum and spinal cord, causing reversible intention tremors ('ryegrass staggers').

questionText: Deoxynivalenol (DON)—a Type B trichothecene mycotoxin produced by Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae) in scabby wheat, barley, and corn—is colloquially known as 'Vomitoxin' because it induces acute feed refusal and emesis, with which domestic species being the most sensitive?
options: Swine (growing and finishing pigs)
Laying hens and broiler chickens
Adult Merino sheep and cashmere goats
Adult beef cattle and water buffaloes
explanation: Swine are by far the most sensitive domestic species to Deoxynivalenol (DON / vomitoxin), showing reduced feed intake at >=1 ppm and complete feed refusal and central serotonin (5-HT3)/peptide YY-mediated emesis at 10–20 ppm, whereas ruminants and poultry degrade DON extensively in the rumen/gut.

questionText: Which nephrotoxic mycotoxin produced by Penicillium citrinum, Penicillium verrucosum, and Aspergillus terreus often co-contaminates stored cereal grains alongside Ochratoxin A, acting synergistically to damage the renal proximal convoluted tubules in pigs and poultry?
options: Zearalenone
Cyclopiazonic acid
Citrinin
Diacetoxyscirpenol (DAS)
explanation: Citrinin is a polyketide nephrotoxin produced by Penicillium and Aspergillus species that frequently co-occurs with Ochratoxin A in temperate cereal grains (barley, oats, corn), causing synergistic degeneration of renal proximal tubules, polydipsia, polyuria, and visceral gout/nephrosis in swine and poultry.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In David Baltimore's classification of viruses based on mRNA synthesis pathways, Class VII viruses (such as Duck Hepatitis B Virus in the family Hepadnaviridae) possess which unique genome and replication strategy?
options: Partially double-stranded circular DNA that replicates via a pregenomic RNA intermediate
Circular single-stranded negative-sense DNA that replicates via rolling-circle amplification in the host nucleolus
Linear single-stranded positive-sense RNA that replicates directly in the cytoplasm without any DNA intermediate
Segmented double-stranded RNA that transcribes monocistronic mRNAs inside an intact icosahedral subviral core
explanation: Baltimore Class VII viruses (Hepadnaviridae and Caulimoviridae, termed pararetroviruses) package a partially double-stranded, gapped circular DNA genome that is repaired to cccDNA in the nucleus, transcribed into pregenomic RNA, and reverse-transcribed back into DNA inside nascent viral cores.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Autonomous Parvoviruses (Baltimore Class II, single-stranded linear DNA) lack a viral DNA polymerase and initiate replication of their genome in the nucleus of S-phase host cells by using:
options: Host transfer RNA (tRNALys or tRNATrp) annealed to a primer-binding site near the 5' end
Self-complementary terminal palindromic sequences
Short host-derived capped mRNA primers cleaved from cellular pre-mRNAs ('cap-snatching')
A covalently linked terminal protein (TP) carrying a deoxycytidine monophosphate residue
explanation: Parvovirus linear ssDNA genomes possess palindromic inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) at both ends that fold back on themselves to form base-paired 3'-OH hairpin duplexes, serving as built-in self-primers for host DNA Polymerase delta.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Why do double-stranded RNA viruses (Baltimore Class III, such as Bluetongue virus, Rotavirus, and Infectious Bursal Disease virus) NEVER uncoat completely to release naked dsRNA into the host cell cytoplasm?
options: Double-stranded RNA spontaneously hydrolyzes at physiological pH 7.4 unless chelated by calcium ions
Naked dsRNA is immediately imported into the host nucleus and integrated by host transposases
The host ribosome directly translates intact dsRNA duplexes without needing mRNA transcription
Exposed cytoplasmic dsRNA is a potent PAMP and host cells lack dsRNA-dependent RNA polymerases
explanation: Eukaryotic cells lack enzymes to transcribe dsRNA into mRNA and possess powerful innate sensors (PKR, RIG-I, MDA5, TLR3, OAS) that trigger interferon and translational shutoff upon detecting naked dsRNA. Therefore, dsRNA viruses keep their genome hidden inside an inner core capsid and extrude only +ssRNA transcripts synthesized by internal viral RdRp.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Unlike cellular mRNAs (which possess a 5' 7-methylguanosine cap), the positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome of Picornaviruses (such as Foot and Mouth Disease Virus) has which structure at its 5' end and initiates translation via which mechanism?
options: A covalently linked tRNA primer and leaky scanning of polycistronic subgenomic mRNAs
A covalently linked viral protein and cap-independent translation
A triphosphorylated 5'-pppA terminus and ribosomal shunting across a hairpin leader
A host-snatched 5' methylated cap and 40S ribosomal scanning from the extreme 5' terminus
explanation: Picornavirus genomic +ssRNA has the small peptide VPg (viral protein genome-linked, encoded by 3B) covalently attached via a tyrosine phosphodiester bond to its 5' uridine, and recruits the 40S ribosome directly to an Internal Ribosome Entry Site (IRES) in the 5' UTR.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: During Foot and Mouth Disease Virus (FMDV) replication, how does the viral Leader Protease (Lpro) rapidly shut off host cell protein synthesis while allowing viral protein synthesis to proceed unimpeded?
options: Lpro depurinates the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit in a manner identical to ricin toxin
Lpro degrades all cellular transfer RNAs (tRNAs) except initiator methionyl-tRNA
Lpro ADP-ribosylates host elongation factor-2 (eEF-2) to freeze polypeptide translocation
Lpro cleaves host eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF4G, abolishing cap-dependent host mRNA translation
explanation: FMDV Leader protease (Lpro, a papain-like cysteine protease) cleaves the host scaffold protein eIF4G (which bridges the 5'-cap-binding protein eIF4E to the 40S ribosome). This shuts down host cap-dependent translation (including Type I interferon synthesis), while FMDV IRES-mediated translation requires only the C-terminal fragment of eIF4G.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: The icosahedral capsid of Foot and Mouth Disease Virus is assembled from 60 copies of each of four structural proteins (VP1, VP2, VP3, and VP4). Which protein is entirely internal (lining the inner capsid surface), and which protein carries the surface-exposed RGD loop that induces neutralizing antibodies?
options: VP1 is entirely internal; VP4 carries the surface RGD neutralizing loop
VP3 is entirely internal; VP2 carries the surface RGD neutralizing loop
Myristoylated; VP1 carries the surface G-H loop with the RGD motif
VP2 is entirely internal; VP3 carries the surface RGD neutralizing loop
explanation: In FMDV (146S intact virion), VP1, VP2, and VP3 form the external icosahedral shell, with the flexible G-H loop of VP1 displaying the conserved Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) tripeptide that binds host alpha-v integrins. VP4 is small, myristoylated, and located entirely on the interior face of the capsid in contact with viral RNA.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In the epidemiology of Foot and Mouth Disease, an animal is defined as a 'Persistent Carrier' if infectious FMDV can be recovered for more than 28 days post-infection. Which domestic species NEVER becomes an FMDV carrier, and what is the primary anatomical site of persistence in cattle (sampled via a Probang cup)?
options: Swine do NOT become carriers; in cattle
Water buffaloes never become carriers; virus persists in the mammary gland of pigs
Cattle never become carriers; virus persists in the renal cortex of pigs
Sheep and goats never become carriers; virus persists in the spleen of horses
explanation: Pigs shed massive aerosol quantities of FMDV ('amplifier hosts') during acute infection but clear the virus completely within 3–4 weeks and NEVER become long-term carriers. Ruminants (cattle up to 3.5 years, sheep ~9 months, African Cape buffalo up to 5 years) harbor persistent virus in the epithelial crypts of the dorsal soft palate and pharynx, sampled via a Probang cup.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In modern commercial FMD vaccine manufacturing, why is Binary Ethylenimine (BEI) universally preferred over Formaldehyde for viral inactivation?
options: BEI cross-links the outer VP1 capsid proteins into rigid heat-stable 12S pentamers
BEI alkylates internal viral RNA with linear first-order kinetics while leaving immunogenic 146S capsid epitopes intact
BEI selectively cleaves the non-structural 3ABC polyprotein from the crude culture supernatant
BEI saponifies the viral lipid envelope without requiring aluminum hydroxide or oil adjuvants
explanation: Formaldehyde cross-links surface capsid proteins and exhibits non-linear ('tailing') inactivation kinetics that can leave residual live virus inside aggregates. Binary Ethylenimine (BEI, an aziridine formed by cyclization of 2-bromoethylamine in alkali) penetrates the capsid and alkylates viral RNA with first-order kinetics without altering the 146S antigenic conformation.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Which emerging picornavirus (genus Senecavirus) causes vesicular lesions on the snout, oral mucosa, and coronary bands of pigs that are clinically indistinguishable from Foot and Mouth Disease, requiring differential RT-PCR in swine vesicular disease investigations?
options: Porcine Teschovirus-1 (Teschen/Talfan disease virus)
Sapelovirus A (Porcine enterovirus 8)
Torque Teno Sus Virus (TTSuV)
Senecavirus A (Seneca Valley Virus)
explanation: Senecavirus A (Seneca Valley Virus, family Picornaviridae) causes acute vesicular lesions on the snout and coronary bands of market pigs and sows as well as neonatal piglet mortality (epidemics since 2015), clinically mimicking FMD, Vesicular Stomatitis, Swine Vesicular Disease, and Vesicular Exanthema of Swine.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Swine Vesicular Disease Virus (SVDV)—which produces vesicular lesions in pigs identical to FMD—differs fundamentally from FMDV in its taxonomy, physicochemical stability, and host range because SVDV is:
options: An Enterovirus that is stable from pH 2.5 to 12.0 and persists in cured pork salami
A double-stranded RNA Orbivirus transmitted biologically by Culicoides biting midges
A Calicivirus derived from marine pinnipeds that is inactivated at 37°C within 1 hour
An enveloped Rhabdovirus that is rapidly destroyed at pH 6.5 and infects horses and cattle
explanation: Swine Vesicular Disease Virus (SVDV) belongs to the genus Enterovirus (species Enterovirus B, closely related to human Coxsackievirus B5). Unlike acid-labile FMDV (inactivated below pH 6.0), SVDV is acid-resistant (stable at pH 2.5–12.0), survives fermentation and smoking in dry sausages for >1 year, and naturally infects only swine.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Encephalomyocarditis Virus (EMCV, genus Cardiovirus, family Picornaviridae) is maintained in nature by commensal rats and mice (Rattus and Mus species) and causes which characteristic fatal syndrome in young swine and captive zoo elephants?
options: Progressive demyelinating leukoencephalomalacia and blindness
Chronic proliferative ileitis and mesenteric lymphadenopathy
Sudden death from acute non-suppurative myocarditis with chalky white necrotic streaks
Vesicular eruptions on the tongue, snout, and interdigital skin
explanation: Rodents are the natural reservoir of EMCV, shedding virus in feces and urine that contaminate swine and elephant feed/water. In piglets and elephants, EMCV has an intense tropism for the myocardium, causing peracute sudden death with pale yellow-to-chalky white calcified necrotic foci in the ventricular myocardium.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: 'Epidemic Tremor' (Avian Encephalomyelitis), characterized by ataxia, sitting on the hocks, rapid fine tremors of the head and neck, and subsequent bilateral lens cataracts in 1-to-3-week-old chicks, is caused by a vertically and horizontally transmitted virus belonging to which family?
options: Flaviviridae (genus Orthoflavivirus)
Picornaviridae
Birnaviridae (genus Avibirnavirus)
Coronaviridae (genus Gammacoronavirus)
explanation: Avian Encephalomyelitis Virus (AEV) is a hepatovirus-like picornavirus (genus Tremovirus). When naive laying hens are infected during egg production, they experience a temporary drop in egg production and transmit the virus vertically into eggs, causing 'Epidemic Tremor' in hatched chicks; breeder pullets are vaccinated at 10–15 weeks (prior to lay).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV / RHDV2)—which causes peracute necrotizing hepatitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), blood-stained nasal discharge, and >80% mortality in European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculi)—belongs to which viral family and genus?
options: Family Filoviridae, genus Orthoebolavirus
Family Togaviridae, genus Alphavirus
Family Caliciviridae, genus Lagovirus
Family Poxviridae, genus Leporipoxvirus
