explanation: Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV / Lagovirus europaeus) is a non-enveloped positive-sense ssRNA virus in the family Caliciviridae (genus Lagovirus) that targets hepatocytes and endothelial cells and characteristically agglutinates human group O erythrocytes.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Among the mosquito-borne equine encephalomyelitis viruses (Eastern [EEE], Western [WEE], and Venezuelan [VEE] Equine Encephalomyelitis viruses, genus Alphavirus, family Togaviridae), which virus uses HORSES as the primary viremic amplifying host rather than a dead-end host?
options: Eastern Equine Encephalomyelitis Virus (EEEV, maintained in Culiseta melanura and passerine birds)
West Nile Virus (WNV, genus Orthoflavivirus)
Western Equine Encephalomyelitis Virus (WEEV, maintained in Culex tarsalis and wild birds)
Venezuelan Equine Encephalomyelitis Virus (VEEV, epidemic strains IA/IB/IC)
explanation: In EEE, WEE, and West Nile virus infections, wild birds are the amplifying reservoir hosts, while horses develop low-level viremia insufficient to infect mosquitoes ('dead-end hosts'). In contrast, epizootic Venezuelan Equine Encephalomyelitis Virus (VEEV) replicates to extremely high viremic titers in horses, making equids the primary amplifying hosts for mosquito transmission.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In the natural transmission cycle of Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV, genus Orthoflavivirus, family Flaviviridae), transmitted by paddy-breeding Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes, which domestic animal serves as the primary mammalian 'amplifying host' (suffering stillbirths, mummified fetuses, and boar orchitis), while horses and humans act as dead-end hosts?
options: Swine
Sheep and goats
Domestic dogs and cats
Domestic cattle and water buffaloes
explanation: Ardeid wading birds (pond herons and cattle egrets) are the natural maintenance reservoirs of JEV, while domestic pigs develop prolonged, high-titer viremia that infects Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes (acting as the key peri-domestic amplifying host). Pregnant sows suffer stillbirths/mummification, whereas horses and humans are dead-end hosts developing fatal encephalitis.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: How does fatal 'Mucosal Disease' (characterized by severe panleukopenia and linear erosions/ulcerations over Peyer's patches and the gastrointestinal tract) develop in cattle infected with Bovine Viral Diarrhea Virus (BVDV)?
options: Superinfection of immunotolerant Persistently Infected animal with antigenically homologous Cytopathic BVDV biotype
Transplacental infection of a fetus during the third trimester (days 200–270) with a cytopathic BVDV strain
Primary post-natal aerosol infection of an immunocompetent adult dairy cow with a non-cytopathic BVDV Type 1 strain
Co-infection of a neonatal calf under 5 days of age with Bovine Coronavirus and Cryptosporidium parvum
explanation: When a fetus is infected between days 40 and 120 of gestation with a Non-Cytopathic (NCP) BVDV strain, it becomes immunotolerant to that specific strain and is born Persistently Infected (PI). If that PI calf later encounters an antigenically homologous Cytopathic (CP) BVDV strain (typically via mutation/RNA recombination that cleaves NS2-3 into NS3), the unchecked CP virus destroys gut lymphoid tissue, causing fatal Mucosal Disease.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Classical Swine Fever Virus (CSFV / Hog Cholera), which envelope glycoprotein is the major immunodominant target of virus-neutralizing antibodies and is incorporated into chimeric or baculovirus-expressed subunit DIVA vaccines?
options: Internal nucleocapsid core protein C (p14)
Envelope glycoprotein Erns (gp44/48, possessing intrinsic ribonuclease activity)
Envelope glycoprotein E2 (gp55)
Non-structural helicase/protease protein NS3 (p80)
explanation: The pestivirus envelope contains three glycoproteins: Erns (secreted ribonuclease used as the companion diagnostic antigen in DIVA ELISAs), E1, and E2. Glycoprotein E2 (gp55) is the major immunogenic surface spike that induces potent neutralizing antibodies and confers complete protection in subunit and chimeric (CP7_E2alf) marker vaccines.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome Virus (PRRSV, family Arteriviridae) exhibits an extremely restricted cellular tropism for porcine alveolar macrophages. Which macrophage surface receptor is the essential mediator of PRRSV uncoating and genome release (whose gene deletion renders gene-edited pigs completely resistant to PRRSV)?
options: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2)
Scavenger receptor CD163
Coxsackievirus and Adenovirus Receptor (CAR)
Signaling Lymphocyte Activation Molecule (SLAM / CD150)
explanation: While sialoadhesin (CD169 / Siglec-1) mediates initial attachment and internalization on porcine alveolar macrophages, the scavenger receptor CD163 (specifically domain 5, SRCR5) is indispensable for PRRSV uncoating and infection; CRISPR/Cas9 pigs lacking CD163 SRCR5 are completely resistant to both PRRSV-1 and PRRSV-2.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Unlike Avian Paramyxoviruses and Orthomyxoviruses, freshly harvested allantoic fluid containing Infectious Bronchitis Virus (IBV, Gammacoronavirus) does NOT spontaneously agglutinate chicken red blood cells until the viral suspension is pre-treated with which enzyme to cleave surface alpha-2,3-linked sialic acid inhibitors?
options: Proteinase K or Papain
Lysozyme or Lysostaphin
Trypsin or Chymotrypsin
Neuraminidase or Phospholipase C
explanation: Native Infectious Bronchitis Virus (IBV) virions do not hemagglutinate chicken erythrocytes directly; treatment of concentrated IBV with bacterial Neuraminidase or Clostridium perfringens Type 1 Phospholipase C removes interfering sialic acid/lipid moieties and exposes the hemagglutinating site on the S1 spike glycoprotein for HI testing.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: According to World Health Organization (WHO) and WOAH standards for human and animal Rabies vaccination, what is the minimum acceptable protective serum virus-neutralizing antibody titer (as measured by RFFIT or FAVN assay) confirming adequate immunity?
options: Greater than or equal to 0.5 IU/mL
Greater than or equal to 10.0 IU/mL
Greater than or equal to 0.01 IU/mL
Greater than or equal to 5.0 IU/mL
explanation: A serum neutralizing antibody level of >= 0.5 International Units per milliliter (0.5 IU/mL), measured by the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT) or Fluorescent Antibody Virus Neutralization (FAVN) test, is the universal benchmark for protective immunity against Rabies.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In clinical differential diagnosis of vesicular diseases, how does Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV, genus Vesiculovirus, family Rhabdoviridae) differ critically in its domestic host range from Foot and Mouth Disease Virus (FMDV)?
options: Vesicular Stomatitis Virus infects only marine pinnipeds and swine, sparing cattle and horses
Vesicular Stomatitis Virus infects only sheep and goats, whereas FMDV infects only horses and dogs
Vesicular Stomatitis Virus causes vesicular lesions exclusively in poultry and waterfowl
Vesicular Stomatitis Virus causes natural clinical vesicular disease in HORSES, whereas horses are refractory to FMDV
explanation: Equids (horses, donkeys, mules) are completely resistant to Foot and Mouth Disease Virus, Swine Vesicular Disease Virus, and Senecavirus A, but are highly susceptible to Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (serotypes New Jersey and Indiana). Therefore, vesicular lesions in horses immediately rule out FMD and point to Vesicular Stomatitis.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Bovine Ephemeral Fever ('Three-Day Sickness')—an arthropod-borne rhabdoviral disease (genus Ephemerovirus) of cattle and water buffaloes characterized by acute biphasic fever, shivering, shifting lameness, and sternal recumbency with rapid recovery—induces recumbency primarily by causing:
options: Massive intravascular hemolysis and methemoglobinemia
Severe acute hypocalcemia and neutrophilic polyserositis
Irreversible demyelination of the sciatic nerve and lumbar spinal cord
Spastic tetanic contraction of axial muscles via Renshaw cell blockade
explanation: Bovine Ephemeral Fever Virus triggers an acute pro-inflammatory cytokine storm (IFN-alpha, TNF-alpha, IL-1) accompanied by a sharp drop in ionized blood calcium (hypocalcemia), causing rumen stasis, muscle tremors, paresis, and recumbency that often responds dramatically to intravenous calcium borogluconate.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In the biological pathotyping of Newcastle Disease Virus (NDV) isolates using 9-to-10-day-old embryonated chicken eggs, how are Velogenic, Mesogenic, and Lentogenic strains classified based on the 'Mean Death Time' (MDT, in hours) of the minimum lethal dose?
options: Velogenic: 100–120 hours; Mesogenic: 120–150 hours; Lentogenic: >150 hours
Velogenic: >90 hours; Mesogenic: 60–90 hours; Lentogenic: <60 hours
Velogenic: <60 hours; Mesogenic: 60–90 hours; Lentogenic: >90 hours
Velogenic: <12 hours; Mesogenic: 12–24 hours; Lentogenic: 24–48 hours
explanation: Mean Death Time (MDT) in embryonated chicken eggs classifies NDV pathotypes into three groups: Velogenic strains kill embryos in <60 hours (ICPI 1.5–2.0); Mesogenic strains (such as R2B Mukteswar and Komarov) kill embryos in 60–90 hours (ICPI 1.0–1.5); and Lentogenic strains (such as LaSota, F, and B1) take >90 hours (ICPI <0.7).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Indian poultry vaccination programs against Newcastle Disease (Ranikhet Disease), which live attenuated 'Mesogenic' strain—administered parenterally (subcutaneously/intramuscularly) as a booster only to birds older than 6 to 8 weeks already primed with a lentogenic vaccine—provides long-lasting immunity?
options: LaSota strain
Ulster 2C strain
Hitchner B1 strain
R2B strain
explanation: The R2B (Mukteswar) strain was developed at IVRI, Mukteswar by serial passage in embryonated eggs. Because it is a mesogenic strain, it is neuropathic/lethal if given to unprimed chicks under 6 weeks of age, and is reserved as an injectable booster at 6–8 weeks after primary lentogenic (F or LaSota) vaccination.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Hendra Virus (causing acute fatal respiratory and neurological disease in horses and humans in Australia) and Nipah Virus (causing 'barking pig syndrome' and fatal human encephalitis in Asia) are BSL-4 zoonotic paramyxoviruses (genus Henipavirus) whose natural wildlife reservoir is:
options: Ixodid hard ticks (Ixodes holocyclus)
Peridomestic brown rats (Rattus norvegicus)
Frugivorous flying foxes
Wild aquatic mallard ducks (Anas platyrhynchos)
explanation: Pteropid fruit bats (flying foxes of the genus Pteropus) are the asymptomatic natural reservoir hosts of both Hendra virus and Nipah virus, shedding virus in urine, saliva, and birthing fluids onto pastures or date palm sap/fruit consumed by horses and pigs.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: During necropsy of a goat or sheep that died of acute Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR), the pathognomonic gross lesion observed along the crests of the longitudinal mucosal folds of the ceco-colic junction and rectum is:
options: Linear dark-red zones of congestion and hemorrhage termed 'Zebra Markings'
Thickened, corrugated, cobblestone-like granulomatous rugae resembling Johne's disease
Annular diphtheritic hemorrhagic rings encircling the gut lumen
Button-like concentric necrotic ulcers ('button ulcers')
explanation: In acute PPR (and historically Rinderpest), linear streaks of severe congestion and hemorrhage develop along the crests of the longitudinal mucosal folds of the posterior colon, ceco-colic junction, and rectum, creating the classic diagnostic appearance known as 'Zebra stripes' or 'Zebra markings'.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Influenza A viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae), what is the specific biological function of the viral Neuraminidase (NA) surface glycoprotein during the replication cycle?
options: It forms a proton-selective ion channel that acidifies the viral core inside the endosome
It cleaves terminal sialic acid residues from host glycoproteins
It snatches 5'-methylated cap structures from host nuclear pre-mRNAs to prime viral transcription
It binds alpha-2,3-sialic acid receptors on host enterocytes to initiate receptor-mediated endocytosis
explanation: While Hemagglutinin (HA) binds sialic acid receptors and mediates membrane fusion, Neuraminidase (NA, a tetrameric mushroom-shaped sialidase) cleaves terminal sialic acid from respiratory mucus and from the infected cell surface, allowing newly budded virions to detach rather than clumping together.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Rift Valley Fever Virus (RVFV, genus Phlebovirus, family Phenuiviridae) is a high-consequence mosquito-borne zoonotic arbovirus in Africa and the Arabian Peninsula whose two classic epidemiological hallmarks in sheep and cattle herds are:
options: Congenital cerebellar hypoplasia and persistent immunotolerant viremia in surviving calves
Vesicular lesions on the coronary band and persistent pharyngeal shedding for 3 years
Chronic progressive carpal arthritis and demyelinating leukoencephalomalacia in adult rams
Nearly 100% 'abortion storms' in pregnant ewes
explanation: Outbreaks of Rift Valley Fever following heavy rainfall and flooding of dambos (Aedes mosquito emergence) are immediately recognized by simultaneous near-100% abortion storms in pregnant ewes/cows, >90% mortality with bright yellow pan-necrotic livers in newborn lambs, and influenza-like/hemorrhagic illness in veterinary personnel.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Akabane Virus and Schmallenberg Virus (genus Orthobunyavirus, family Peribunyaviridae) are Culicoides-transmitted arboviruses that cause mild or subclinical infection in adult cattle and sheep, but when transmitted transplacentally during early-to-mid gestation, they cause which classic congenital malformation syndrome?
options: Arthrogryposis-Hydranencephaly Syndrome
Hypomyelinogenesis ('hairy shaker lambs') and persistent postnatal viremia syndrome
Osteopetrosis ('marble bone disease') and thymic aplasia syndrome
Bilateral microphthalmia, persistent right aortic arch, and ventricular septal defects syndrome
explanation: Akabane virus, Schmallenberg virus, and Cache Valley virus are teratogenic orthobunyaviruses transmitted by Culicoides midges (or mosquitoes for Cache Valley). Depending on the gestational age of the fetus, destruction of developing cerebral neuroblasts and spinal ventral horn motor neurons produces Hydranencephaly and neurogenic Arthrogryposis (AHS).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Nairobi Sheep Disease Virus (genus Orthonairovirus, family Nairoviridae)—which causes peracute hemorrhagic gastroenteritis and >70% mortality in naive sheep and goats in East Africa—is antigenically and genetically synonymous with which tick-borne virus found in India?
options: Kyasanur Forest Disease Virus (transmitted by Haemaphysalis spinigera)
Chandipura Virus (transmitted by Phlebotomus sandflies)
Ganjam Virus (transmitted in India by Haemaphysalis intermedia)
Bhanja Virus (transmitted by Rhipicephalus decoloratus)
explanation: Nairobi Sheep Disease Virus (transmitted in East Africa by the brown ear tick Rhipicephalus appendiculatus) and Ganjam Virus (isolated from sheep and goats in Odisha/India and transmitted by Haemaphysalis intermedia) are now classified as variants of the same Orthonairovirus species (Nairobi sheep disease orthonairovirus).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In the double-layered icosahedral capsid of Bluetongue Virus (BTV, genus Orbivirus), which structural protein forms the conserved middle core layer (detecting all 29+ BTV serotypes in group-specific cELISA), and which outer capsid protein determines the specific Serotype (1–29+) in Virus Neutralization?
options: VP6 is the group-specific core antigen; VP4 is the serotype-specific outer neutralization antigen
VP7 is conserved group-specific middle core antigen; VP2 is outer capsid protein determining serotype specificity
NS1 is the group-specific core antigen; NS3 is the serotype-specific outer neutralization antigen
VP2 is the group-specific core antigen; VP7 is the serotype-specific outer neutralization antigen
explanation: In Bluetongue Virus, VP7 (encoded by segment 7) forms the 260 trimers of the middle core layer and is highly conserved across all BTV serotypes (serving as the target antigen in competitive ELISA). VP2 (encoded by segment 2) forms the outermost triskelion spikes, mediates hemagglutination and cell attachment, and determines serotype specificity.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: African Horse Sickness Virus (AHSV, genus Orbivirus) manifests in four classical clinical forms in equids. What are the pathognomonic signs of the peracute 'Dunkop' form versus the subacute 'Dikkop' form?
options: Dunkop is characterized by hepatic cirrhosis; Dikkop is characterized by ulcerative lymphangitis
Dunkop is the cutaneous papular form; Dikkop is the hemorrhagic enterocolitis form
Dunkop causes fulminant pulmonary edema
Dunkop is the mild fever form in zebras; Dikkop is the ascending spinal paralysis form
explanation: In Afrikaans, 'Dunkop' ('thin head', the peracute pulmonary form) is characterized by severe dyspnea, paroxysmal coughing, and copious frothy yellow fluid pouring from the nostrils (>95% mortality). 'Dikkop' ('thick head', the subacute cardiac form) is characterized by hydropericardium and dramatic gelatinous subcutaneous edema bulging out the supraorbital fossae, eyelids, and neck (~50% mortality).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Group A Rotaviruses (family Sedoreoviridae)—a premier cause of neonatal diarrhea in calves, piglets, and foals—possess 11 segments of dsRNA and encode which non-structural glycoprotein that acts as the first discovered 'Viral Enterotoxin' by mobilizing intracellular Ca2+?
options: NSP4 (Non-structural protein 4, encoded by segment 10)
VP7 (Outer capsid glycoprotein G-type antigen)
VP4 (Protease-cleaved spike protein P-type antigen)
VP6 (Middle capsid group-specific protein, encoded by segment 6)
explanation: Rotavirus Non-Structural Protein 4 (NSP4) is an endoplasmic reticulum transmembrane glycoprotein and secreted enterotoxin peptide that binds integrin receptors on uninfected crypt cells, activates phospholipase C / IP3, elevates cytosolic Ca2+, and stimulates chloride secretion via calcium-activated chloride channels.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Infectious Bursal Disease (Gumboro Disease) of chickens, why does infection of chicks BEFORE 2 weeks of age produce catastrophic lifelong humoral immunosuppression (vaccine failures against NDV/IBV) with minimal clinical mortality, whereas infection at 3 to 6 weeks of age produces acute clinical disease, bursal hemorrhage, and high mortality?
options: Chicks under 2 weeks express no viral receptors in the bursa and replicate virus only in the brain
Chicks under 2 weeks possess mature CD8+ cytotoxic T cells that lyse the thymus instead of the bursa
IBDV replicates exclusively in bone marrow erythroblasts during the first 14 days post-hatch

IBDV destroys actively dividing immature IgM+ B-lymphocyte precursors in Bursa of Fabricius, permanently ablating B-cell repertoire in neonates while triggering massive cytokine storm in 3-to-6-week-old chicks
explanation: The target cell of IBDV is the actively dividing surface-IgM-bearing (sIgM+) immature B-lymphocyte in the cloacal Bursa of Fabricius. In chicks <2 weeks old, destruction of bursal stem cells prevents seeding of peripheral lymphoid organs (permanent B-cell immunodepletion without severe clinical inflammation). At 3–6 weeks, when the bursa is maximally populated with sIgM+ B cells, massive synchronous cytolysis triggers acute cytokine storm, coagulopathy, and mortality.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: How is Equine Infectious Anemia Virus (EIAV, genus Lentivirus) transmitted between horses in the field, and which viral core protein is used as the antigen in the official Coggins Agar Gel Immunodiffusion (AGID) test?
options: Transmitted biologically by Culicoides midges; Coggins test detects envelope glycoprotein gp90
Transmitted mechanically
Transmitted venereally by carrier stallions; Coggins test detects reverse transcriptase p66
Transmitted transovarially by Rhipicephalus ticks; Coggins test detects matrix protein p15
explanation: EIAV is transmitted mechanically via interrupted blood feeding by painful large biting flies (horseflies [Tabanus], deerflies [Chrysops], and stable flies [Stomoxys]) or contaminated needles. Because envelope gp90/gp45 undergo rapid antigenic drift causing recurrent febrile waves, the Coggins AGID test uses the highly conserved major capsid core protein p26.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Small Ruminant Lentiviruses (Maedi-Visna Virus in sheep and Caprine Arthritis Encephalitis Virus in goats) evade host neutralizing antibodies and disseminate into the lungs, mammary gland, joints, and CNS via which classic cellular mechanism coined by Ashley Haase?
options: Erythrocyte surface adsorption via viral hemagglutinin spikes
Retrograde axonal transport inside peripheral sensory nerve fibers
Free cell-free viremia Complexed with host alpha-2-macroglobulin
The 'Trojan Horse' mechanism
explanation: Maedi-Visna Virus (MVV) and CAEV infect bone marrow myeloid precursors and circulating blood monocytes, where viral transcription is restricted ('silent' provirus, evading immune detection)—the classic 'Trojan Horse' mechanism. Only when monocytes migrate into target tissues (lung, udder, synovium, choroid plexus) and mature into macrophages does full viral gene expression occur.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In poultry oncology, how is Lymphoid Leukosis (caused by Avian Leukosis Virus, an Alpharetrovirus) pathologically and epidemiologically differentiated from Marek's Disease (caused by Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2)?
options: Lymphoid Leukosis is a B-cell lymphoma originating
Lymphoid Leukosis is caused by a DNA herpesvirus shed in feather dander; Marek's Disease is caused by an RNA retrovirus transmitted vertically in egg albumen
Lymphoid Leukosis is a T-cell lymphoma causing sciatic nerve paralysis in 4-week-old chicks; Marek's Disease is a B-cell lymphoma restricted to hens >24 weeks old
Lymphoid Leukosis produces intranuclear Cowdry Type A inclusions in tracheal epithelium; Marek's Disease produces Bollinger bodies in skin
explanation: Key differential table: Marek's Disease (Alphaherpesvirus) transforms CD4+ T-cells (via Meq), affects young birds (>=3–4 weeks), causes enlargement/yellowing and loss of cross-striations of peripheral nerves (sciatic/brachial plexus) and diffuse bursal atrophy. Lymphoid Leukosis (Alpharetrovirus) transforms IgM+ B-cells via insertional activation of c-myc inside the Bursa of Fabricius (producing nodular bursal tumors), occurs only in sexually mature birds (>16 weeks), and NEVER involves peripheral nerves.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Which subgroup of exogenous Avian Leukosis Virus (ALV)—which emerged in the late 1980s through recombination with endogenous retroviral env sequences—exhibits a unique tropism for myeloid cells and causes 'Myelocytomatosis' (chalky-white tumors on the sternum, ribs, pelvis, and liver) in meat-type broiler breeders?
options: Avian Leukosis Virus Subgroup A (ALV-A)
Avian Leukosis Virus Subgroup E (ALV-E, endogenous locus ev)
Avian Leukosis Virus Subgroup J (ALV-J)
Reticuloendotheliosis Virus (REV)
explanation: While classical exogenous ALV subgroups A and B induce B-cell lymphoid leukosis in egg-type layers, ALV Subgroup J (ALV-J) possesses a divergent gp85 envelope glycoprotein (binding the chicken Na+/H+ exchanger 1, chNHE1) and predominantly induces myeloid leukosis (myelocytomatosis) in meat-type broiler breeders.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In point-of-care veterinary diagnostics for feline retroviruses, what specific viral target is detected by the in-clinic ELISA/immunochromatography test for Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) versus Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV)?
options: FeLV test detects proviral DNA by agglutination; FIV test detects p27 antigen in tears
FeLV test detects free soluble p27 core capsid ANTIGEN in blood; FIV test detects host ANTIBODIES against viral p24
FeLV test detects anti-gp70 antibodies; FIV test detects free reverse transcriptase antigen
Both FeLV and FIV point-of-care tests detect only host IgM antibodies in saliva
explanation: Viremic FeLV-infected cats shed large excesses of unencapsidated major core protein p27 into plasma, so FeLV rapid tests are sandwich assays detecting p27 ANTIGEN. Conversely, FIV-infected cats have very low plasma viral antigen loads after the acute phase, so FIV rapid tests are indirect/competitive assays detecting anti-FIV ANTIBODIES (against p24 capsid or gp40 transmembrane protein).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Why can a live attenuated Goatpox vaccine (such as the Uttarkashi strain used in India) or Sheeppox vaccine be used for heterologous immunization of cattle against Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD)?
options: Lumpy Skin Disease virus is actually a Parapoxvirus that shares its envelope with Orf virus
Lumpy Skin Disease is caused by Bovine Herpesvirus-2, which cross-reacts with Goatpox virus
Goatpox virus integrates into the bovine chromosome via reverse transcriptase virus
Sheeppox virus and Goatpox virus
explanation: All three members of the genus Capripoxvirus—Sheeppox virus (SPPV), Goatpox virus (GTPV), and Lumpy Skin Disease virus (LSDV)—cannot be distinguished serologically by virus neutralization and share >96% nucleotide sequence identity, providing strong cross-protection (alongside homologous attenuated LSDV Neethling vaccines).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Contagious Ecthyma ('Orf', 'Scabby Mouth', or 'Contagious Pustular Dermatitis') of sheep and goats is caused by a Parapoxvirus whose virions are immediately distinguished from Orthopoxviruses and Capripoxviruses under negative-stain electron microscopy by their:
options: Icosahedral capsid surrounded by a spiked double lipid envelope resembling a wheel
Bullet-shaped helical nucleocapsid with a flat base and rounded apex
Narrow ovoid shape with surface protein tubules wound in regular criss-cross spiral pattern
Long filamentous pleomorphic rods measuring over 1,000 nm in length
explanation: Whereas Orthopoxviruses and Capripoxviruses are large brick-shaped virions (250 x 300 nm) with randomly arranged short surface tubules ('mulberry' form), Parapoxviruses (Orf virus, Pseudocowpox virus, Bovine Papular Stomatitis virus) are smaller, oval/cocoon-shaped (160 x 260 nm) with a single continuous surface tubule wrapped spirally creates a diagnostic criss-cross ('ball of wool') pattern.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In histopathological sections of avian skin infected with Fowlpox Virus (genus Avipoxvirus), hyperplastic and ballooning epidermal prickle cells contain large, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies termed:
options: Bollinger bodies
Negri bodies (containing Lyssavirus ribonucleoprotein)
Cowdry Type A bodies (characteristic of Infectious Laryngotracheitis virus)
Guarnieri bodies (characteristic of Vaccinia and Cowpox viruses)
explanation: Avipoxviruses (Fowlpox, Pigeonpox, Canarypox, Turkeypox) induce massive epidermal hyperplasia containing pathognomonic large, eosinophilic, lipid-rich intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called Bollinger bodies; when crushed and stained (e.g., Gimenez or Wright stain), Bollinger bodies release individual viral elementary bodies known as Borrel bodies.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Control and eradication programs for Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis (BHV-1) and Pseudorabies / Aujeszky's Disease (SuHV-1) in Europe and North America utilize 'Marker Vaccines' (DIVA vaccines) engineered by deleting which non-essential viral envelope glycoprotein gene?
options: Glycoprotein D (gD, which is essential for high-affinity receptor binding)
Glycoprotein E (gE, formerly designated gI in Pseudorabies virus)
Major capsid protein VP5 (UL19, which forms the icosahedral hexons and pentons)
Glycoprotein B (gB, which is essential for viral cell-to-cell fusion and entry)
explanation: In both Bovine Alphaherpesvirus 1 (BHV-1) and Suid Alphaherpesvirus 1 (Pseudorabies virus), Glycoprotein E (gE, which complexes with gI to facilitate anterograde axonal spread and cell-to-cell spread) is non-essential for replication in vitro, but is expressed by 100% of wild-type field strains. Deleting the gE gene yields a safe attenuated vaccine whose recipients remain negative on an anti-gE blocking ELISA.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Marek's Disease of chickens (caused by Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2), although CD4+ T-lymphocytes in visceral tumors and peripheral nerves are latently infected and transformed by the viral 'Meq' oncogene, where is the ONLY anatomical site in the chicken where productive replication of fully enveloped, cell-free infectious virions occurs for horizontal shedding?
options: The keratinizing Feather Follicle Epithelium, shed
The goblet cells of the cecal tonsils and duodenum
The Schwann cells of the sciatic and brachial nerve plexuses
The cortical lymphocytes of the Bursa of Fabricius
explanation: In lymphoid cells and tumors, Marek's Disease Virus is strictly cell-associated and non-infectious if cells are lysed. Productive lytic replication producing fully enveloped, cell-free, environmentally stable infectious virions occurs EXCLUSIVELY in the stratified squamous Feather Follicle Epithelium (FFE), which sloughs off as infectious feather dander/poultry house dust.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Vaccination against Marek's Disease is routinely performed at the hatchery (either in ovo at day 18 of embryonation or subcutaneously at day 1 of age). How are the three serotypes of Marek's Disease-related avian herpesviruses defined?
options: Serotype 1: Lentogenic NDV; Serotype 2: Mesogenic NDV; Serotype 3: Velogenic NDV
Serotype 1: Herpesvirus of Turkeys (HVT); Serotype 2: Infectious Laryngotracheitis virus; Serotype 3: Duck Plague virus
Serotype 1: Avian Leukosis virus; Serotype 2: Reticuloendotheliosis virus; Serotype 3: Chicken Anemia virus
Serotype 1: Oncogenic MDV & attenuated CVI988
explanation: Marek's disease viral group comprises three serotypes: Serotype 1 (Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2) includes all pathogenic/oncogenic field strains and their attenuated derivatives (most notably the gold-standard CVI988 / Rispens vaccine strain); Serotype 2 (Gallid alphaherpesvirus 3) includes naturally non-oncogenic chicken strains (SB-1, 301B/1); and Serotype 3 (Meleagrid alphaherpesvirus 1) is the apathogenic Herpesvirus of Turkeys (HVT, FC126).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: 'Egg Drop Syndrome 1976' (EDS-76)—characterized by a sudden drop in egg production and laying of pale, thin-shelled, soft-shelled, or shell-less eggs by apparently healthy hens—is caused by Duck Atadenovirus A (family Adenoviridae), which is diagnostically unique among avian adenoviruses because it:
options: Causes 100% mortality with hydropericardium ('Leechi disease') in 3-week-old broilers
Directly agglutinates chicken, duck, and turkey erythrocytes
Replicates exclusively in the cytoplasm and produces Bollinger bodies
Contains a segmented double-stranded RNA genome and requires Culicoides vectors
explanation: Unlike classical Fowl Aviadenoviruses (FAdV-1 to 12, most of which do not hemagglutinate chicken RBCs), EDS-76 virus (Duck Atadenovirus A) strongly agglutinates avian (chicken, duck, turkey, goose) erythrocytes via its fiber knob protein, making the Hemagglutination Inhibition (HI) test the standard serological assay.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: 'Hydropericardium Syndrome' ('Angara Disease' or 'Leechi Disease') in 3-to-6-week-old broiler chickens—characterized by sudden mortality (up to 60%), accumulation of clear straw-colored jelly-like fluid in the pericardial sac (giving the heart the appearance of a peeled leechi fruit), and multifocal hepatic necrosis with basophilic intranuclear inclusions—is caused by:
options: Avian Reovirus (Orthoreovirus)
Duck Atadenovirus A (Egg Drop Syndrome-76 virus)
Fowl Aviadenovirus Serotype 4
Chicken Anemia Virus (Gyrovirus)
explanation: First reported at Angara Goth near Karachi (1987) and termed 'Leechi disease' in India, Hydropericardium-Hepatitis Syndrome is caused specifically by virulent strains of Fowl Adenovirus Serotype 4 (FAdV-4, species Fowl aviadenovirus C), whereas other serotypes (FAdV-2, -8a, -8b, -11) cause classic Inclusion Body Hepatitis (IBH) without severe hydropericardium.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In cattle chronically grazing pastures infested with Bracken Fern (Pteridium aquilinum), which Bovine Papillomavirus (BPV) type acts synergistically with bracken fern carcinogens (ptaquiloside) and quercetin to induce urinary bladder tumors (hemangiomas and transitional cell carcinomas) causing 'Enzootic Bovine Hematuria'?
options: Bovine Papillomavirus Type 8
Bovine Papillomavirus Type 3 (cutaneotropic Xipapillomavirus)
Bovine Papillomavirus Type 2
Bovine Papillomavirus Type 6 (teat frond papillomavirus)
explanation: Bracken fern contains the immunosuppressant and DNA-alkylating norsesquiterpene glucoside Ptaquiloside. In cattle grazing bracken fern, latent Bovine Papillomavirus Type 2 (BPV-2, a Deltapapillomavirus that also causes equine sarcoids along with BPV-1) is activated in the urothelium and vascular endothelium to cause Enzootic Bovine Hematuria, while BPV-4 causes esophageal/ruminal squamous cell carcinoma.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In gilts and sows exposed oronasally during the first half of pregnancy (before fetal immunocompetence at day 70 of gestation), Porcine Parvovirus (PPV) crosses the placenta and spreads sequentially from fetus to fetus along the uterine horn, causing which classic reproductive syndrome in the absence of maternal illness?
options: SMEDI Syndrome (Stillbirth, Mummification, Embryonic Death, and Infertility)
Blue Ear Disease with late-term abortion at day 110 and maternal anorexia/cyanosis
Maternal agalactia, vulvovaginitis, and rectal prolapse
Congenital Myoclonia Congenita ('dancing pig disease') and cerebellar hypoplasia
explanation: Porcine Parvovirus (Ungulate protoparvovirus 1) causes no clinical signs in the pregnant dam, but transplacental infection before day 30 causes embryonic death and resorption (return to service/infertility), infection between days 30 and 70 causes sequential fetal death and mummification of fetuses of progressively different sizes (SMEDI), and fetuses infected after day 70 mount an antibody response and survive.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Aleutian Mink Disease Virus (AMDV, genus Amdoparvovirus, family Parvoviridae) causes a fatal chronic wasting disease in mink and ferrets whose immunopathogenesis is a textbook model of:
options: Prion-like amyloid conversion of host neuronal membrane proteins
Non-neutralizing hypergammaglobulinemia and extreme plasmacytosis
Complete aplasia of the thymus and Bursa of Fabricius with agammaglobulinemia
IgE-mediated systemic anaphylaxis and mast cell degranulation
explanation: In adult mink (especially homozygous recessive Aleutian 'aa' mink), AMDV replicates in macrophages and stimulates massive polyclonal B-cell activation and hypergammaglobulinemia (>50% of serum protein is anti-viral IgG). Instead of neutralizing the virus, these antibodies mediate Fc-receptor uptake into macrophages (ADE) and deposit in renal glomeruli and arteries as fatal Type III immune complexes.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Chicken Anemia Virus (CAV, genus Gyrovirus, family Anelloviridae) is vertically transmitted from breeder flocks that become infected during egg production and causes 'Blue Wing Disease' in 2-to-3-week-old progeny chicks by selectively destroying which two precursor cell populations?
options: Cerebellar Purkinje neurons and pancreatic acinar cells
Bursal B-lymphocytes and intestinal crypt enterocytes
Tracheal ciliated epithelial cells and renal tubular epithelium
Bone marrow hemocytoblasts and cortical thymocytes
explanation: Chicken Anemia Virus possesses a circular negative-sense ssDNA genome encoding the apoptin protein (VP3), which selectively induces apoptosis in dividing bone marrow erythroblast/granulocyte/thrombocyte progenitors (hemocytoblasts, causing profound anemia, watery blood, fatty yellow femoral marrow, and subcutaneous hemorrhages) and T-lymphocyte precursors in the thymic cortex.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (Prion diseases such as Scrapie and BSE), the conformational conversion of normal host cellular prion protein (PrPC) into the infectious pathogenic isoform (PrPSc) involves which fundamental change in secondary protein structure without any change in amino acid sequence?
options: Covalent cross-linking of cysteine residues to bacterial lipopolysaccharide
Enzymatic glycosylation and phosphorylation of tyrosine residues by viral kinases
Post-translational refolding of alpha-helical domains into protease-resistant beta-sheet aggregates
Cleavage of the C-terminal GPI anchor and refolding from beta-sheets into 100% alpha-helices
explanation: Normal PrPC and infectious PrPSc have the exact same primary amino acid sequence encoded by the host PRNP gene. However, PrPC is monomeric, rich in alpha-helices (~42% alpha-helix, 3% beta-sheet), and completely degraded by Proteinase K, whereas PrPSc acts as a conformational template that refolds PrPC into insoluble fibrils rich in beta-sheets (~43% beta-sheet) whose PrP27-30 core resists Proteinase K.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Genetic susceptibility and resistance of domestic sheep to classical Scrapie is controlled by polymorphisms at three specific codons (136, 154, and 171) of the ovine prion protein gene (PRNP). Which haplotype/genotype confers the highest genetic resistance (targeted by national Scrapie eradication breeding programs), and which confers the highest susceptibility?
options: VRQ/VRQ confers maximal resistance; ARR/ARR confers maximal susceptibility
ARR/ARR confers maximal resistance; VRQ/VRQ confers maximal susceptibility
All sheep genotypes are equally susceptible regardless of codons 136, 154, and 171
ARQ/ARH confers maximal resistance; AHQ/AHQ confers maximal susceptibility
explanation: In the ovine 3-codon PRNP classification (codons 136 [A/V], 154 [R/H], and 171 [R/Q/H]): the ARR allele (Alanine-136, Arginine-154, Arginine-171) confers dominant resistance to classical scrapie (homozygous ARR/ARR rams are Type 1 resistant), whereas the VRQ allele (Valine-136, Arginine-154, Glutamine-171) confers extreme susceptibility.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: For statutory post-mortem surveillance and confirmatory diagnosis of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle and Scrapie in sheep, which specific anatomical region of the brainstem must be harvested (often via the foramen magnum using a specialized spoon) because it is the earliest and most consistent site of vacuolar change and PrPSc accumulation?
options: The Obex region of the medulla oblongata
The Ammon's horn of the hippocampus and cerebellar vermis
The lumbar spinal cord intumescence and dorsal root ganglia
The olfactory bulbs and prefrontal cerebral cortex
explanation: Following oral ingestion of prions, PrPSc ascends from the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (ileal Peyer's patches) via parasympathetic fibers of the vagus nerve and sympathetic splanchnic nerves directly to the Dorsal Motor Nucleus of the Vagus (DMNV) located at the level of the Obex in the medulla oblongata, making the obex the mandatory regulatory diagnostic sample.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: How does Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) of deer, elk, and moose differ epidemiologically from Classical Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle?
options: CWD is caused by a slow lentivirus rather than a Proteinase K-resistant prion protein
CWD prions are restricted strictly to the brain and never enter lymphoid tissues
CWD is transmitted exclusively via contaminated meat-and-bone meal and never spreads horizontally
Via environmental contamination because PrPCWD accumulates extensively in peripheral lymphoid tissues
explanation: In Classical BSE of cattle, PrPSc is largely restricted to the CNS, retina, and distal ileum (Specified Risk Materials), so BSE is not contagious horizontally between cattle and spreads only via contaminated feed. In contrast, CWD in cervids (and classical Scrapie in sheep) exhibits widespread lymphoid replication (tonsils, retropharyngeal lymph nodes, Peyer's patches) and is shed in saliva, urine, feces, and placenta, maintaining horizontal transmission.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Which non-retroviral animal negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus (Order Mononegavirales, family Bornaviridae)—the causative agent of fatal non-suppurative meningoencephalomyelitis ('Sad Horse Disease') with intranuclear Joest-Degen inclusion bodies in horses and sheep—is unique because it replicates and transcribes its genome inside the HOST CELL NUCLEUS?
options: Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (genus Vesiculovirus)
Newcastle Disease Virus (genus Orthoavulavirus)
Rabies Virus (genus Lyssavirus)
Borna Disease Virus 1
explanation: Unlike Rhabdoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, and Filoviridae (which replicate exclusively in the cytoplasm), Borna Disease Virus (BoDV-1, reservoired in the bicolored white-toothed shrew Crocidura leucodon) replicates and transcribes its -ssRNA genome inside the host cell nucleus, utilizes host nuclear RNA splicing machinery, and forms eosinophilic intranuclear Joest-Degen inclusion bodies in hippocampal neurons.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Duck Virus Enteritis ('Duck Plague', caused by Anatid alphaherpesvirus 1), necropsy of affected ducks reveals which pathognomonic gross lesions in the gastrointestinal tract?
options: Annular hemorrhagic bands
Massive dilation of the proventriculus filled with undigested seeds without intestinal hemorrhage
Multiple nodular B-cell tumors in the Bursa of Fabricius and osteopetrosis of the tibiotarsus
Zebra-striped linear hemorrhages restricted strictly to the rectum and spiral colon
explanation: Duck Virus Enteritis (Duck Plague, an alphaherpesvirus) has a strong tropism for vascular endothelium and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, producing pathognomonic dark-red annular bands ('hemorrhagic rings') around the four annular lymphoid rings of the duck small intestine (or raised diphtheritic discs in Pekin ducks) and diphtheritic membranes along the longitudinal folds of the esophagus.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Avian Orthoreoviruses (family Reoviridae), the causative agents of 'Viral Arthritis / Tenosynovitis' (rupture of the gastrocnemius tendon above the hock joint) in broiler chickens, are non-enveloped dsRNA viruses that nevertheless induce massive syncytia (cell-cell fusion) in cell culture by expressing which unique viral protein?
options: An internal myristoylated VP4 capsid protein that lyses host nuclei
A hemagglutinin-esterase (HE) dimer that degrades plasma membrane cholesterol
Small non-structural Fusion-Associated Small Transmembrane protein designated p10
A furin-cleaved enveloped F0 fusion glycoprotein spike
explanation: Fusogenic orthoreoviruses (such as Avian Reovirus and Nelson Bay Reovirus) lack a lipid envelope and have no structural fusion spikes; instead, they encode a tiny (~10 kDa) non-structural membrane-spanning protein called p10 (a FAST protein: Fusion-Associated Small Transmembrane protein) that traffics to the infected cell plasma membrane and drives cell-to-cell syncytium formation.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV, genus Orthonairovirus, family Nairoviridae) is a high-fatality BSL-4 zoonotic pathogen transmitted primarily by Hyalomma ticks. What is the clinical manifestation of CCHFV infection in domestic ruminants (cattle, sheep, and goats)?
options: Severe vesicular lesions on the tongue, dental pad, and interdigital cleft
Subclinical infection with a 1-week viremia
Progressive hindlimb paralysis and hydropericardium ('heartwater')
Nearly 100% mortality with bloody diarrhea, necrotic stomatitis, and corneal opacity
explanation: In cattle, sheep, goats, and ostriches, Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus causes an inapparent (subclinical) infection with transient viremia lasting ~7 days. Domestic ruminants thus serve as silent amplifying hosts that infect feeding Hyalomma ticks and expose veterinarians and abattoir workers via viremic blood.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Duck Viral Hepatitis Type 1 (DHV-1, genus Avihepatovirus, family Picornaviridae) causes peracute, high-mortality (>90%) infection in young ducklings under 3 weeks of age, characterized clinically and pathologically by:
options: Cystic dilatation of the right oviduct and laying of rough-shelled depigmented eggs
Chronic bumblefoot, amyloidosis of the spleen, and diphtheritic esophagitis
Sudden death in characteristic 'opisthotonos' with enlarged, pale liver covered in punctate
Slow progressive paralysis of the legs with enlargement of the sciatic nerves
explanation: Duck Viral Hepatitis Type 1 (Duck Hepatitis A Virus-1, family Picornaviridae) strikes ducklings <3 weeks old with peracute spasmodic paddling and death within an hour in classic opisthotonos (head drawn back over the dorsum), accompanied by an enlarged reddish-yellow liver studded with petechial and ecchymotic hemorrhages.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Vesicular Exanthema of Swine Virus (VESV, genus Vesivirus, family Caliciviridae)—which caused FMD-like vesicular outbreaks in pigs fed raw garbage in California—originated from a marine reservoir virus endemic in Pacific pinnipeds known as:
options: Elephant Endotheliotropic Herpesvirus (EEHV)
San Miguel Sea Lion Virus (SMSV)
Phocine Distemper Virus (PDV)
Cetacean Morbillivirus (CeMV)
explanation: Vesicular Exanthema of Swine Virus (VESV, family Caliciviridae) is phylogenetically and antigenically a strain of San Miguel Sea Lion Virus (SMSV) that jumped from marine pinnipeds (sea lions, fur seals) and opaleye fish into swine herds fed uncooked marine offal in swill.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: 'Louping Ill'—an acute tick-borne viral encephalomyelitis of sheep and red grouse in the British Isles characterized by a biphasic fever and a peculiar bounding, leaping cerebellar ataxia ('louping' gait)—is caused by an Orthoflavivirus transmitted by:
options: Ixodes ricinus (castor bean / sheep tick)
Ornithodoros moubata (soft tampan tick)
Rhipicephalus appendiculatus (brown ear tick)
Dermacentor reticulatus (ornate cow tick)
explanation: Louping Ill Virus belongs to the Tick-Borne Encephalitis (TBE) complex in the genus Orthoflavivirus (family Flaviviridae) and is biologically transmitted on heather moorlands by the three-host hard tick Ixodes ricinus, causing fatal polioencephalomyelitis in sheep and willow ptarmigan/red grouse.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In Classical Swine Fever (Hog Cholera), which live attenuated vaccine strain (adapted by hundreds of serial passages in rabbits) is the global gold-standard vaccine, and what is the most pathognomonic gross lesion seen in the spleen of pigs dying of acute CSF?
options: Sungri-96 strain; complete atrophy and fibrosis of the splenic white pulp
Neethling strain; rupture of the splenic capsule with hemoperitoneum
Mukteswar strain; diffuse splenomegaly with miliary caseous granulomas
Lapinized Chinese strain; raised, dark-red wedge-shaped marginal infarcts along edges of spleen
explanation: The lapinized Chinese ('C') strain of CSFV induces rapid, lifelong immunity within 3–5 days of vaccination. At necropsy of acute Classical Swine Fever, raised dark-red pyramidal infarcts along the margin of the spleen (caused by fibrinoid necrosis of splenic arterioles), 'turkey-egg' petechiated kidneys, and colonic 'button ulcers' are pathognomonic.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: 'Vomiting and Wasting Disease' (VWD) in suckling piglets under 3 weeks of age—characterized by repeated retching, emaciation, constipation, and encephalomyelitis—is caused by Porcine Hemagglutinating Encephalomyelitis Virus (PHEV), which belongs to:
options: Family Arteriviridae, genus Betaarterivirus
Family Circoviridae, genus Circovirus
Family Picornaviridae, genus Enterovirus
Family Coronaviridae, genus Betacoronavirus
explanation: Porcine Hemagglutinating Encephalomyelitis Virus (PHEV) is a Betacoronavirus (expressing a Hemagglutinin-Esterase [HE] glycoprotein that agglutinates chicken/mouse RBCs) that replicates in nasal/tonsillar mucosa and spreads retrogradely via the trigeminal and vagus nerves to the medullary vomiting center and Auerbach's myenteric plexus of the stomach.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: While the surface Glycoprotein (G) of Rabies virus is the sole antigen that induces virus-neutralizing antibodies, which internal structural protein is the most abundant, highly conserved group-specific antigen targeted by FITC-conjugated antibodies in the gold-standard Direct Fluorescent Antibody Test (dFAT) on brain impression smears?
options: Matrix protein (M protein, which lines the inner surface of the viral envelope)
Nucleoprotein (N protein, which encapsidates the genomic RNA
Large protein (L protein, the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase)
Phosphoprotein (P protein, the non-catalytic polymerase cofactor)
explanation: Rabies virus Nucleoprotein (N) tightly encapsidates the viral RNA and forms the bulk of the cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein aggregates (Negri bodies). Because the N protein is produced in vast excess and is antigenically conserved across Lyssavirus genotypes, anti-N monoclonal antibodies conjugated to FITC are used in the direct FAT.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Peste des Petits Ruminants Virus (PPRV) and Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) (genus Morbillivirus) infect host lymphocytes (causing profound acute leukopenia and lymphoid depletion) and subsequently infect mucosal epithelial cells (for horizontal shedding) by binding sequentially to which two host cell-surface receptors?
options: SLAM on immune cells, followed by Nectin-4 on epithelial cells
CD4 on T-helper cells, followed by CCR5 on mucosal macrophages cells
Sialoadhesin (CD169) on macrophages, followed by CD163 in endosomes cells
Alpha-v-beta-6 integrin on tongue epithelium, followed by heparan sulfate cells
explanation: All Morbilliviruses (Measles, Rinderpest, PPRV, CDV) use SLAM (CD150) expressed on activated T- and B-lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells as their primary immune receptor (explaining severe morbillivirus-induced immunosuppression), and subsequently use the adherens junction protein Nectin-4 (PVRL4) on the basolateral surface of respiratory/intestinal epithelium for viral exit.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In dogs with acute Canine Distemper, microscopic examination of Giemsa- or Wright-stained peripheral blood smears, conjunctival scrapings, or urinary bladder transitional epithelium frequently reveals eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies known specifically as:
options: Joest-Degen bodies
Councilman bodies
Lentz bodies
Guarnieri bodies
explanation: In Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) infection, aggregates of viral nucleocapsid tubules form characteristic round-to-ovoid acidophilic (eosinophilic) intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called 'Lentz bodies' inside circulating neutrophils, lymphocytes, erythrocytes, and transitional epithelial cells of the urinary bladder and renal pelvis.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: During Influenza A virus entry into a host cell following receptor-mediated endocytosis, what is the critical function of the viral Matrix-2 (M2) envelope protein (the target of the antiviral drug Amantadine)?
options: It cleaves alpha-2,6-sialic acid receptors to release the virion from respiratory mucus
It polymerizes complementary positive-sense cRNA templates inside the nucleolus
It forms a proton-selective ion channel
It exports newly synthesized viral mRNAs out of the host cell nucleus via CRM1
explanation: The Influenza A M2 protein is a tetrameric transmembrane proton (H+) channel (viroporin). Inside the acidified late endosome (pH 5.0–6.0), M2 conducts protons into the virion core, disrupting the interaction between Matrix protein M1 and the 8 viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) segments so that the vRNPs are released into the cytosol after HA-mediated membrane fusion.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Reticuloendotheliosis Virus (REV, genus Gammaretrovirus) causes runting-stunting syndrome, feathering defects ('Nakanuke'), and lymphomas in poultry, and is uniquely notorious in veterinary vaccine quality control because its proviral DNA can naturally integrate into the genome of which two large avian DNA viruses?
options: Fowlpox Virus (Avipoxvirus) and Marek's Disease Virus (Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2)
Infectious Bursal Disease Virus (Birnavirus) and Avian Reovirus
Chicken Anemia Virus (Gyrovirus) and Goose Parvovirus
Newcastle Disease Virus (Paramyxovirus) and Infectious Bronchitis Virus (Coronavirus)
explanation: Reticuloendotheliosis Virus (REV) is an avian gammaretrovirus whose reverse-transcribed LTRs or full-length provirus can spontaneously insert into the large double-stranded DNA genomes of Fowlpox virus and Marek's Disease virus during co-infection of birds or embryo fibroblast cultures, historically causing widespread REV contamination of commercial Fowlpox and HVT vaccines.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Myxoma Virus (genus Leporipoxvirus, family Poxviridae) is a classic textbook example of host-parasite co-evolution. It causes only a benign, localized cutaneous fibroma in its natural reservoir (South American tapeti / Sylvilagus brush rabbits), whereas in European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculi) it causes:
options: Peracute necrotizing hepatitis and epistaxis within 24 hours without skin nodules
Fulminant generalized 'Myxomatosis'
Chronic demyelinating encephalitis and cataracts after a 2-year incubation period
Subclinical lifelong enteric shedding without any skin lesions
explanation: Introduced into Australia in 1950 to control feral European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculi) and transmitted mechanically by mosquitoes and the rabbit flea (Spilopsyllus cuniculi), Myxoma virus caused >99.8% case fatality in naive Oryctolagus rabbits, before co-evolving toward intermediate virulence Rank III/IV strains alongside rising rabbit genetic resistance.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Bovine Alphaherpesvirus 1 (BHV-1) is divided into restriction-endonuclease subtypes (BHV-1.1, BHV-1.2a, and BHV-1.2b). While BHV-1.1 causes classical respiratory Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis (IBR / 'Red Nose'), which clinical venereal syndromes are caused by BHV-1.2b?
options: Epivaginitis and fibropapillomatosis of the glans penis
Malignant Catarrhal Fever and corneoscleral panvasculitis
Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia and ulcerative mammillitis
Infectious Pustular Vulvovaginitis in cows
explanation: The exact same virus species—Bovine alphaherpesvirus 1 (BHV-1)—causes both respiratory disease (IBR, primarily subtype 1.1) and venereal genital disease: Infectious Pustular Vulvovaginitis (IPV) in cows and Infectious Pustular Balanoposthitis (IPB) in bulls (primarily subtype 1.2b, which does not cause abortion).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: In laying and breeder chickens, acute Infectious Laryngotracheitis (caused by Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1) is clinically and pathologically characterized by gasping ('pump-handle breathing'), expectoration of blood-stained mucus casts, and which pathognomonic histopathological lesion in the tracheal mucosa during the first 1–5 days?
options: Sloughing multinucleated epithelial syncytia containing eosinophilic intranuclear Cowdry Type inclusion bodies
Granulomatous giant-cell pneumonia with dichotomously branching hyphae
Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic Bollinger bodies inside hyperplastic squamous cells
Crypt epithelial necrosis with large basophilic amphophilic inclusions in Peyer's patches
explanation: Infectious Laryngotracheitis Virus (ILTV, Gallid alphaherpesvirus 1) replicates strictly in the respiratory epithelium and conjunctiva (establishing latency in the trigeminal ganglion), inducing fusion of respiratory epithelial cells into multinucleated syncytia that contain prominent eosinophilic intranuclear Cowdry Type A inclusion bodies.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Malignant Catarrhal Fever (MCF) is a fatal, sporadic lymphoproliferative and necrotizing panvasculitis of cattle, water buffaloes, bison, and deer. Which two reservoir species asymptomatically harbor and shed the causative gammaherpesviruses—Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1 (AlHV-1) and Ovine gammaherpesvirus 2 (OvHV-2), respectively?
options: African Cape buffalo (Syncerus caffer) for AlHV-1, and domestic goats (Capra hircus) for OvHV-2
Plains zebras for AlHV-1, and red deer for OvHV-2
Dromedary camels for AlHV-1, and wild boars for OvHV-2
Blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus) for AlHV-1, and domestic sheep (Ovis aries) for OvHV-2
explanation: Wildebeest-associated MCF (WA-MCF) in Africa is caused by Alcelaphine gammaherpesvirus 1 (AlHV-1), shed in nasal/ocular secretions of young wildebeest calves up to 3–4 months of age. Sheep-associated MCF (SA-MCF) worldwide is caused by Ovine gammaherpesvirus 2 (OvHV-2), carried asymptomatically by domestic sheep (especially lambs aged 6–9 months); affected cattle are dead-end hosts.

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Which bovine herpesvirus causes 'Bovine Herpes Mammillitis' (severe painful vesicles, plaques, and ulcers on the teats and udder skin of first-calf dairy heifers) as well as generalized benign 'Pseudo-Lumpy Skin Disease'?
options: Bovine Alphaherpesvirus 5 (BHV-5, agent of bovine necrotizing meningoencephalitis)
Bovine Alphaherpesvirus 2 (BHV-2 / Allerton virus)
Bovine Alphaherpesvirus 1 (BHV-1)
Bovine Gammaherpesvirus 4 (BHV-4 / Movar virus)
explanation: Bovine Alphaherpesvirus 2 (BHV-2, antigenically related to human Herpes Simplex Virus) replicates best at lower skin temperatures (30–35°C) and causes two distinct syndromes: localized ulcerative Bovine Herpes Mammillitis on the teats/udder of periparturient dairy heifers, and generalized superficial skin nodules termed Pseudo-Lumpy Skin Disease (Allerton virus).

topic: General & Systematic Virology (DNA & RNA Animal/Poultry Viruses & Prions)
questionText: Bovine Papillomavirus Types 1 and 2 (BPV-1 and BPV-2, genus Deltapapillomavirus) are unique among all known mammalian papillomaviruses because they can cross the species barrier to infect dermal fibroblasts of horses, donkeys, and mules, causing the most common equine skin tumor known as:
options: Equine Cutaneous Melanomatosis
Equine Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the third eyelid
Equine Sarcoid
Equine Molluscum Contagiosum
explanation: Unlike strict epitheliotropic papillomaviruses, Deltapapillomaviruses (BPV-1 and BPV-2) infect both epithelium and subepithelial fibroblasts (fibropapillomas in cattle). When transmitted to equids via flies or fomites, BPV-1/BPV-2 non-productively transform equine dermal fibroblasts via the E5 and E6/E7 oncoproteins, producing locally aggressive Equine Sarcoids.

questionText: In calves, lambs, and piglets, the continuous 'Ileal Peyer's Patch' (unlike the discrete jejunal Peyer's patches) functions during fetal and early neonatal life as a:
options: Primary lymphoid organ for antigen-independent B-cell repertoire diversification prior to involution
Purely endocrine organ secreting thymosin and erythropoietin into portal blood
Filtration bed for senescent erythrocytes and intravascular hemosiderin storage
Secondary lymphoid organ dedicated exclusively to CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell memory maintenance
explanation: In ruminants, swine, and dogs (the 'GALT species'), the large continuous Ileal Peyer's Patch develops prenatally without exogenous antigen, mediates primary B-cell diversification (via somatic hypermutation/gene conversion), and involutes by sexual maturity—functioning as a primary lymphoid organ analogous to the avian Bursa of Fabricius.

questionText: In comparative veterinary anatomy and immunology, lymph nodes of SWINE (as well as hippopotamuses and dolphins) are structurally unique among domestic mammals because they are:
options: Filled with circulating red blood cells instead of lymph fluid ('hemal nodes')
Anatomically 'inverted'
Located exclusively inside the lumen of the appendix and cecal tonsils
Completely absent and replaced by nucleated thrombocytes in the spleen
explanation: Porcine lymph nodes have an 'inverted' microarchitecture: afferent lymphatics enter at the hilus-like capsule to deliver antigen to centrally located cortical B-cell follicles, while the medulla is on the outer periphery. Furthermore, recirculating porcine lymphocytes exit the lymph node directly into post-capillary High Endothelial Venules (HEVs) into the blood rather than via efferent lymphatics.

questionText: In poultry immunology, which paraocular secondary lymphoid gland—located behind the third eyelid within the orbit and densely populated with IgA- and IgG (IgY)-secreting plasma cells—is the primary site of local mucosal immunity following eye-drop vaccination against Newcastle Disease or Infectious Bronchitis?
options: The Cloacal Bursa of Fabricius gland
Meckel's diverticulum of the jejunum gland
The Pineal gland of the epithalamus gland
The Harderian gland
explanation: The Harderian gland is the dominant paraocular lymphoid organ in birds, located ventromedial to the eyeball. It contains massive accumulations of B-lineage plasma cells and T cells that mount rapid local secretory IgA and IgY responses across the conjunctiva and upper respiratory tract after eye-drop or spray vaccination.

questionText: In avian B-lymphocyte development inside the Bursa of Fabricius, unlike humans and mice (which generate antibody diversity primarily through combinatorial V-D-J joining of hundreds of V segments), chickens possess only a single functional V and J segment and generate their entire primary antibody repertoire via:
options: Alternative mRNA splicing of twenty constant-region exons
Horizontal transfer of maternal immunoglobulin mRNA from egg albumen
Somatic 'Gene Conversion'
Cytoplasmic reverse transcription of endogenous retroviral LTRs
explanation: Chickens (as well as rabbits and cattle to a degree) rearrange only a single functional VH1 and VL1 gene segment; inside the Bursa of Fabricius, Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase (AID) drives somatic Gene Conversion, copying hypervariable stretches from an upstream array of non-functional V-pseudogenes into the rearranged V gene.

questionText: In the innate immune system, Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) of the Toll-Like Receptor (TLR) family recognize conserved microbial PAMPs. Which pairing of Toll-Like Receptor and its specific microbial ligand is CORRECT?
options: TLR1: Chitin; TLR4: Mycolic acid; TLR7: Dipicolinic acid; TLR9: Ergosterol
TLR2: viral ssRNA; TLR3: Lipoteichoic acid; TLR4: Flagellin; TLR5: Peptidoglycan
TLR4: viral dsRNA; TLR5: CpG DNA; TLR3: bacterial Flagellin; TLR9: Gram-negative LPS
TLR4: Gram-negative LPS; TLR5: Flagellin; TLR3: viral dsRNA; TLR9: unmethylated CpG DNA
explanation: Canonical TLR specificity: TLR4 (with MD-2 and CD14) senses Gram-negative Lipopolysaccharide (Lipid A); TLR5 senses bacterial Flagellin; TLR2 (heterodimerized with TLR1 or TLR6) senses lipopeptides, peptidoglycan, and lipoteichoic acid; endosomal TLR3 senses viral dsRNA; TLR7/8 sense viral ssRNA; and endosomal TLR9 senses unmethylated CpG DNA.

questionText: While Toll-Like Receptors scan the cell surface and endosomes, which cytosolic Nucleotide-binding Oligomerization Domain (NOD)-like receptor specifically senses 'Muramyl Dipeptide' (MDP)—the minimal bioactive peptidoglycan motif found in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and Freund's Complete Adjuvant?
options: NOD2
cGAS (Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase)
MDA5 (Melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5)
RIG-I (Retinoic acid-inducible gene I)
explanation: NOD1 senses gamma-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelic acid (iE-DAP, specific to Gram-negative peptidoglycan), whereas NOD2 is a general cytosolic sensor of Muramyl Dipeptide (MurNAc-L-Ala-D-isoGln, MDP), conserved in all bacterial peptidoglycans and the active immunostimulatory motif of mycobacteria in FCA.

questionText: During the oxygen-dependent 'Respiratory Burst' inside the phagolysosome of activated neutrophils, which enzyme complex first reduces molecular oxygen (O2) to superoxide anion (O2.-), and which granule enzyme then uses hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and chloride ions (Cl-) to generate potent bactericidal Hypochlorous Acid (HOCl)?
options: Catalase generates superoxide; Lysozyme generates hypochlorous acid
Xanthine oxidase generates superoxide; Lactoferrin generates hypochlorous acid
NADPH oxidase (Phox) generates superoxide; Myeloperoxidase (MPO) generates hypochlorous acid
Cytochrome c oxidase generates superoxide; Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) generates HOCl
explanation: Upon phagocytosis, the membrane-bound NADPH oxidase complex (gp91phox/p22phox + p47/p67/Rac) transfers electrons from NADPH to O2, forming superoxide (O2.-), which dismutates to H2O2. Azurophilic granule Myeloperoxidase (MPO) then catalyzes H2O2 + Cl- + H+ -> HOCl (hypochlorous acid/bleach) + H2O.

questionText: According to Klas Kärre's 'Missing-Self Hypothesis', how do Natural Killer (NK) cells selectively spare healthy host cells while lysing virus-infected cells (such as herpesvirus-infected cells) and tumor cells?
options: NK cells phagocytose only bacteria coated with IgE and eosinophil major basic protein cells
NK cells express inhibitory receptors that engage self MHC Class I on normal cells
NK cells require prior immunization and recognize viral peptides bound to MHC Class II cells
NK cells express rearranged T-cell receptor alpha-beta chains that bind free viral capsids cells
explanation: NK cells integrate signals from activating receptors (recognizing stress ligands like MICA/ULBPs or IgG Fc via CD16) and dominant inhibitory receptors (KIRs, Ly49, CD94/NKG2A) that bind normal self MHC Class I. When viruses evade CD8+ T cells by downregulating MHC Class I, they remove the inhibitory brake on NK cells, triggering exocytosis of Perforin and Granzyme B.

questionText: Differentiation of naive CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes into specialized effector lineages (Th1, Th2, Th17, and regulatory Treg cells) is governed by lineage-defining 'Master Transcription Factors'. Which pairing of T-helper subset and its master transcription factor is CORRECT?
options: Th1: T-bet; Th2: GATA-3; Th17: ROR-gamma-t; Treg: FoxP3
Th1: GATA-3; Th2: T-bet; Th17: FoxP3; Treg: ROR-gamma-t
Th1: Bcl-6; Th2: NFAT; Th17: c-Myc; Treg: p53
Th1: FoxP3; Th2: ROR-gamma-t; Th17: STAT1; Treg: GATA-3
explanation: Lineage-defining master transcription factors of CD4+ T cells: Th1 (induced by IL-12/IFN-gamma) expresses T-bet; Th2 (induced by IL-4) expresses GATA-3; Th17 (induced by TGF-beta + IL-6/IL-23) expresses RORgt; Follicular helper Tfh expresses Bcl-6; and Regulatory T cells (Treg, CD4+CD25+) express FoxP3.

questionText: In mucosal immunology and helminth infections, which cytokine—secreted by Th2 lymphocytes and Group 2 Innate Lymphoid Cells (ILC2s)—serves as the principal hematopoietin driving bone marrow differentiation, activation, and survival of Eosinophils, and which cytokine drives B-cell class switching to mucosal IgA?
options: Interleukin-2 drives eosinophils; Interferon-gamma drives IgA class switching
Interleukin-12 drives eosinophils; Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha drives IgA class switching
Interleukin-17 drives eosinophils; Interleukin-1 beta drives IgA class switching
Interleukin-5 drives eosinophil production
explanation: Interleukin-5 (IL-5) is the master eosinophilopoietin responsible for peripheral blood and tissue eosinophilia in parasitic infections and allergies. In Peyer's patches and mucosal lymphoid tissues, Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-beta) induces B-cell heavy-chain class switching to IgA, while IL-5 and IL-6 promote terminal differentiation into IgA-secreting plasma cells.

questionText: In the endogenous MHC Class I antigen presentation pathway, after cytosolic viral proteins are degraded into 8-to-10-amino-acid peptides by the immunoproteasome, how are these peptides translocated across the membrane of the Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) to load onto MHC Class I molecules?
options: By binding to the Invariant chain (CD74) and endosomal sorting via clathrin pits
Via passive diffusion through outer membrane OmpF porin channels
By active ATP-dependent transport through the heterodimeric TAP complex
By exocytosis into the extracellular fluid followed by pinocytosis into the Golgi apparatus
explanation: Peptides generated in the cytosol by the 26S immunoproteasome (LMP2/LMP7) are actively pumped into the lumen of the Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum by the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) heterodimer TAP (TAP1 + TAP2), where tapasin, calreticulin, and ERp57 load them into the MHC Class I alpha-chain + beta-2-microglobulin groove.

questionText: In the exogenous MHC Class II antigen presentation pathway, why do newly synthesized MHC Class II alpha-beta heterodimers inside the Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum NOT accidentally bind endogenous cytosolic peptides present in the ER?
options: Endogenous peptides carry a positive charge that is repelled by MHC Class II
The peptide-binding groove of MHC Class II
MHC Class II molecules remain unfolded until secreted outside the plasma membrane
MHC Class II molecules are synthesized exclusively inside lysosomes rather than the ER
explanation: Inside the ER, trimers of the Invariant Chain (Ii / CD74) associate with nascent MHC Class II alpha-beta dimers, inserting the CLIP (Class II-associated Invariant chain Peptide) region directly into the peptide-binding groove to block endogenous peptide binding and guide the complex to acidified MIIC endolysosomes, where cathepsins cleave Ii and DM catalyzes exchange of CLIP for exogenous peptide.

questionText: Which non-classical MHC Class I-like family of antigen-presenting molecules (associated with beta-2-microglobulin) possesses a deep hydrophobic binding groove specialized for presenting microbial LIPID and GLYCOLIPID antigens (such as mycobacterial mycolic acids and lipoarabinomannan) to T cells and iNKT cells?
options: TAP1/TAP2 peptide transporters
FcRn (Neonatal Fc receptors)
CD1 molecules
CD28 costimulatory homodimers
explanation: Whereas classical MHC Class I and Class II molecules present linear peptide antigens, the non-polymorphic CD1 family of glycoproteins features a deep, non-polar hydrophobic pocket that binds the fatty acyl chains of mycobacterial lipids (mycolic acids, glucose monomycolate, lipoarabinomannan), presenting their hydrophilic headgroups to T cells and invariant NKT (iNKT) cells.

questionText: In comparative veterinary immunology, young ruminants (calves, lambs, kids) and young pigs are classified as 'Gamma-Delta (gd) T-cell High' species (in contrast to 'gd-Low' humans, mice, and dogs) because in young calves and piglets:
options: Gamma-delta T lymphocytes constitute 30% to 60% of circulating peripheral blood T cells
Gamma-delta T cells secrete all circulating serum IgG1 and IgM antibodies cells
Gamma-delta T cells are restricted exclusively to the brain and never enter blood cells
Alpha-beta T cells are completely absent due to physiological thymic aplasia cells
explanation: In humans, mice, and dogs, gamma-delta (gd) T cells account for <5% of peripheral blood lymphocytes. In contrast, ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats), pigs, and chickens are 'gd-high' species where gd T cells (many expressing the Workshop Cluster 1 [WC1] transmembrane scavenger receptor) comprise 30–60% of circulating T cells in young animals, acting as rapid MHC-unrestricted sentinels at mucosae.

questionText: According to the Two-Signal Model of naive T-lymphocyte activation, what happens if a naive T cell receives Signal 1 (TCR-CD3 binding to peptide-MHC on an APC) in the COMPLETE ABSENCE of Signal 2 (costimulatory binding of T-cell CD28 to CD80/CD86 [B7-1/B7-2] on the APC)?
options: The T cell switches its TCR from alpha-beta to gamma-delta and lyses the APC
The T cell immediately differentiates into a long-lived memory plasma cell
The T cell undergoes rapid polyclonal proliferation and secretes massive amounts of IL-2
T cell enters state of prolonged antigen-specific functional unresponsiveness termed 'Clonal Anergy'
explanation: Signal 1 (TCR-CD3 + CD4/CD8 engaging peptide-MHC) provides antigen specificity, while Signal 2 (CD28 engaging B7.1 [CD80] / B7.2 [CD86] induced on PRR-activated professional APCs) is mandatory to stabilize IL-2 mRNA and drive proliferation. Receiving Signal 1 alone without Signal 2 induces peripheral tolerance via Clonal Anergy.

questionText: Bacterial 'Superantigens' (such as Staphylococcus aureus Enterotoxins A–E, Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 [TSST-1], and Streptococcus pyogenes SpeA) trigger a massive, life-threatening cytokine storm (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-2, IFN-gamma) by:
options: Being endocytosed, cleaved into 9-mer peptides, and presented by MHC Class I to 0.001% of CD8+ T cells
Binding intact outside peptide-binding groove to cross-link conserved V-beta domain of TCR to alpha-chain of MHC Class II, polyclonally activating up to 20% of all T cells
Binding directly to Toll-like receptor 4 and CD14 on polymorphonuclear neutrophils cells
Cleaving the Fc region of secretory IgA and activating the alternative complement pathway cells
explanation: Conventional peptide antigens sit inside the MHC groove and activate only ~0.0001–0.001% of T cells bearing a matching CDR3. Superantigens are intact proteins that clamp onto the outside lateral surfaces of MHC Class II and specific V-beta families of the TCR, non-specifically activating 5–20% of the entire T-cell repertoire simultaneously.

questionText: In classical immunochemistry implemented by Rodney Porter and Alfred Nisonoff, how does proteolytic digestion of an intact IgG molecule with 'Papain' differ from digestion with 'Pepsin'?
options: Papain cleaves above the hinge disulfide bonds to yield two monovalent Fab fragments
Papain yields a single divalent F(ab')2 fragment; Pepsin yields two monovalent Fab fragments and an intact Fc
Papain cleaves only the interchain disulfide bonds to separate intact heavy chains from light chains
Pepsin leaves the Fc complement-binding domain completely intact while destroying both antigen-binding sites
explanation: Papain cleaves the IgG heavy chain on the N-terminal side (above) of the hinge inter-heavy-chain disulfide bridge, producing two separate monovalent Fab fragments (which bind antigen but cannot precipitate/agglutinate) and one crystalline Fc fragment. Pepsin cleaves on the C-terminal side (below) of the hinge disulfide bonds, keeping the two Fab arms linked as a divalent F(ab')2 fragment (used in commercial equine tetanus/snake antivenoms to neutralize toxin without causing Fc-mediated serum sickness).

questionText: In immunoglobulin genetics and serology, what is the precise distinction between an 'Isotype', an 'Allotype', and an 'Idiotype'?
options: Isotypes occur only in IgM; Allotypes occur only in IgA; Idiotypes occur only in IgE
Isotypes are encoded by RAG-1; Allotypes are generated by somatic hypermutation; Idiotypes are located on the Fc tail
Isotype is an individual's unique paratope; Allotype is the heavy chain class; Idiotype is an allelic polymorphism
Isotypes are constant-region classes
explanation: Isotypes (e.g., IgG1, IgG2, IgM, IgA, IgE) are defined by constant-region genes present in the genome of every normal member of a species.
